regions.name: Primary Visual Cortex (V1)
regions.one_liner: The first cortical stop for vision; builds a retinotopic map of edges, contrast and orientation.
functions: Retinotopic mapping of the visual field
Edge, contrast and orientation detection (simple/complex cells)
Feeds the ventral ('what') and dorsal ('where/how') visual streams
regions.lesion_effects: Damage causes a scotoma (blind patch) in the corresponding part of the visual field; bilateral destruction causes cortical blindness, sometimes with 'blindsight' — unconscious residual visual responding via spared subcortical routes.
regions.approx_location: Posterior pole of the occipital lobe, along the calcarine sulcus, bilateral.
regions.famous_case_or_evidence: Blindsight patients (e.g., patient D.B., studied by Weiskrantz) respond to stimuli in a subjectively 'blind' field, showing vision without V1-based awareness.

regions.name: Visual Area V4
regions.one_liner: Ventral-stream specialist for color constancy and intermediate shape/form.
functions: Feeds object- and face-recognition areas downstream
regions.lesion_effects: Damage can cause cerebral achromatopsia — loss of color perception (the world looks gray) despite otherwise intact vision and acuity.
regions.approx_location: Ventral occipito-temporal cortex, anterior to V1/V2, bilateral.

regions.name: Middle Temporal Area (MT/V5)
regions.one_liner: Dorsal-stream motion specialist computing direction and speed of moving stimuli.
regions.lesion_effects: Bilateral damage produces akinetopsia ('motion blindness') — the world appears as a series of static snapshots rather than continuous motion.
regions.approx_location: Posterior temporal cortex at the temporo-parieto-occipital junction, bilateral.
regions.famous_case_or_evidence: Patient L.M. (Zihl, von Cramon & Mai, 1983) with bilateral MT-area damage could not perceive continuous motion (e.g., poured liquid looked frozen in successive positions).

regions.name: Fusiform Face Area (FFA)
regions.one_liner: Specializes in fast, holistic recognition of individual faces (and, in an adjacent patch, visual word forms).
functions: Face detection and holistic/configural structural encoding
Discriminating individual identities from facial structure
Generates the face-selective N170 ERP response
regions.lesion_effects: Damage causes prosopagnosia (face blindness) — inability to recognize familiar faces by sight, while other object recognition and person identification via voice/gait can remain intact.
regions.approx_location: Lateral fusiform gyrus, ventral temporal lobe, with a right-hemisphere bias.
regions.famous_case_or_evidence: Simultaneous fMRI-EEG work (Gao et al., 2019, Psychophysiology) source-localizes the N170 face response to the fusiform gyrus/FFA; acquired prosopagnosia cases confirm the region's necessity for face identity.

regions.name: Primary Auditory Cortex (A1)
regions.one_liner: First cortical relay for sound, mapping sound frequency tonotopically.
functions: Basic pitch, loudness and timing encoding
Feeds language (Wernicke's area) and auditory 'what/where' streams
regions.lesion_effects: Unilateral damage causes only mild contralateral hearing deficits (because subcortical relays are bilateral); bilateral destruction can cause cortical deafness.
regions.approx_location: Superior temporal gyrus / Heschl's gyrus, bilateral.

regions.name: Wernicke's Area
regions.one_liner: Supports language comprehension — turning heard or read words into meaning.
functions: Semantic access for words and sentences
Monitoring one's own speech for sense
regions.lesion_effects: Causes Wernicke's (fluent/receptive) aphasia: fluent, grammatical-sounding but often meaningless speech (paraphasias, neologisms) with poor comprehension; patients are often unaware of their own errors.
regions.approx_location: Posterior superior temporal gyrus, left hemisphere in roughly 95-99% of right-handers.
regions.famous_case_or_evidence: Carl Wernicke's 1874 description of patients with fluent but incoherent speech and poor comprehension, contrasting with Broca's earlier cases.

regions.name: Broca's Area
regions.one_liner: Supports speech production and grammatical sentence construction.
functions: Coordinating language output with motor cortex
regions.lesion_effects: Causes Broca's (non-fluent/expressive) aphasia: slow, effortful, agrammatic ('telegraphic') speech with relatively preserved comprehension; patients are typically aware of and frustrated by the deficit.
regions.approx_location: Posterior inferior frontal gyrus (pars opercularis/triangularis), typically left hemisphere.
regions.famous_case_or_evidence: Paul Broca's patient 'Tan' (Leborgne, 1861) could only utter the syllable 'tan' but understood language, localizing expressive speech to the left frontal lobe.

regions.name: Primary Somatosensory Cortex (S1)
regions.one_liner: Maps touch, pressure, temperature and body position onto a distorted 'body map' (the sensory homunculus).
regions.lesion_effects: Causes contralateral loss of fine touch/proprioception and astereognosis (inability to identify objects by touch alone); pain/temperature sensation is more diffusely represented and less selectively lost.
regions.approx_location: Postcentral gyrus, parietal lobe, immediately posterior to the central sulcus.

regions.name: Primary Motor Cortex (M1)
regions.one_liner: Generates direct commands for voluntary, skilled movement via a somatotopic 'motor homunculus'.
functions: Major origin of the corticospinal tract
regions.lesion_effects: Causes contralateral weakness or paralysis (hemiparesis/hemiplegia), classically from stroke; some recovery can occur over time via plasticity in surrounding cortex.
regions.approx_location: Precentral gyrus, frontal lobe, immediately anterior to the central sulcus.

regions.name: Posterior Parietal Cortex (PPC)
regions.one_liner: Integrates senses to build a spatial map of body and world, guiding attention and reaching.
regions.lesion_effects: Right PPC damage (especially right inferior parietal lobule/temporo-parietal junction) classically causes hemispatial neglect — inattention to the left side of space despite intact vision and no primary sensory loss.
regions.approx_location: Posterior parietal lobe around the intraparietal sulcus; spatial-attention functions are often right-lateralized.
regions.famous_case_or_evidence: Classic neglect patients fail to draw the left half of a clock or eat food from the left side of a plate (reviewed in Heilman & Mesulam's work on neglect).

regions.name: Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex (dlPFC)
regions.one_liner: Executive-control hub: holds information in mind, plans, and flexibly switches strategies.
regions.lesion_effects: Causes 'dysexecutive syndrome': poor planning, perseveration (e.g., impaired Wisconsin Card Sorting performance), and working-memory deficits, while personality and social behavior are relatively spared (contrast with vmPFC damage).
regions.approx_location: Lateral surface of the frontal lobe, anterior to premotor cortex, bilateral.

regions.name: Ventromedial Prefrontal Cortex / Orbitofrontal Cortex (vmPFC/OFC)
regions.one_liner: Assigns emotional/subjective value to options and integrates 'gut feeling' into decisions.
functions: Value-based decision making (a 'common currency' for comparing options)
Regulating impulse control and social behavior
regions.lesion_effects: Causes impaired real-life decision-making and personality change (impulsivity, poor foresight, blunted social/emotional judgment) despite normal IQ and intact working memory.
regions.approx_location: Ventral and medial surface of the frontal lobe, above the orbits.
regions.famous_case_or_evidence: Phineas Gage (1848 railroad-spike injury to ventromedial/orbitofrontal cortex) showed dramatic personality change; Damasio's 'somatic marker hypothesis' patients (e.g., patient EVR) show similar real-world decision deficits despite intact intellect.

regions.name: Anterior Cingulate Cortex (ACC)
regions.one_liner: Monitors conflict and errors, and links effort and pain to motivation.
regions.lesion_effects: Bilateral damage can cause akinetic mutism — profound apathy and reduced spontaneous movement/speech despite preserved physical ability; partial damage can blunt error sensitivity and motivation.
regions.approx_location: Medial frontal cortex, wrapping around the anterior corpus callosum.

regions.name: Insula
regions.one_liner: The body's interoceptive hub — senses internal states and links them to emotion.
functions: Integrating bodily state with subjective feeling and risk perception
regions.lesion_effects: Linked to impaired disgust recognition/experience and altered risk-taking (reduced 'gut feeling' warning signals); insular stroke can also disrupt pain/temperature perception or cardiac regulation.
regions.approx_location: Folded deep within the lateral sulcus, between the frontal, temporal and parietal opercula.

regions.name: Corpus Callosum
regions.one_liner: The brain's largest fiber bridge, carrying information between the left and right hemispheres.
functions: Interhemispheric transfer of sensory, motor and cognitive information
regions.lesion_effects: Surgical section ('split-brain') or damage causes disconnection syndromes — e.g., an object felt only by the left hand cannot be verbally named, because right-hemisphere information can't reach left-hemisphere language areas.
regions.approx_location: Midline, beneath the cingulate cortex, arching between the two cerebral hemispheres.
regions.famous_case_or_evidence: Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga's split-brain patient studies (1960s-70s; Sperry received the 1981 Nobel Prize) revealed hemisphere-specific processing.

regions.name: Thalamus
regions.one_liner: The brain's central relay and gatekeeper, routing almost all sensory (and some motor) signals to cortex.
functions: Sensory relay to cortex (vision via LGN, hearing via MGN, touch via VPL/VPM)
Motor relay from basal ganglia/cerebellum to M1
Regulating arousal and consciousness via thalamocortical loops
regions.lesion_effects: Can cause contralateral sensory loss and thalamic pain syndrome (Dejerine-Roussy syndrome — chronic burning pain); damage to intralaminar/central nuclei can impair arousal and consciousness, even causing coma.
regions.approx_location: Paired egg-shaped structures deep in the brain's center, flanking the third ventricle.

regions.name: Hypothalamus
regions.one_liner: The body's homeostasis control center — regulating hunger, thirst, temperature, sleep drive and hormones.
functions: Control of the pituitary/endocrine axis (HPA axis)
Circadian rhythm coordination via the suprachiasmatic nucleus
regions.lesion_effects: Damage to specific nuclei produces distinct syndromes: classic animal studies show ventromedial hypothalamus lesions cause overeating/obesity and lateral hypothalamus lesions reduce feeding; human hypothalamic damage (e.g., tumors) can cause obesity, temperature dysregulation, or disrupted sleep-wake cycles.
regions.approx_location: Below the thalamus, above the brainstem, surrounding the floor of the third ventricle.

regions.name: Amygdala
regions.one_liner: Rapid threat/emotional-salience detector, central to fear learning and emotional memory tagging.
functions: Emotional salience tagging of memories (modulates hippocampal consolidation)
regions.lesion_effects: Bilateral damage impairs recognition of fear in others' faces and reduces the subjective experience/physiological expression of fear, while other emotions remain more intact.
regions.approx_location: Almond-shaped nucleus in the anterior medial temporal lobe, just anterior to the hippocampus.
regions.famous_case_or_evidence: Patient S.M. (Urbach-Wiethe disease causing bilateral amygdala calcification), studied by Adolphs & Tranel, showed impaired fear recognition and reduced real-world fear, though she could still be induced to panic via CO2 inhalation — showing the amygdala isn't the sole fear pathway.

regions.name: Hippocampus
regions.one_liner: Forms new explicit (episodic/declarative) memories and supports spatial navigation, then gradually 'teaches' them to cortex.
functions: Sharp-wave ripple replay during sleep for consolidation
regions.lesion_effects: Bilateral damage causes profound anterograde amnesia — inability to form new long-term declarative memories — while procedural/skill learning and short-term/working memory remain intact; old, well-consolidated memories are often relatively preserved (temporally graded retrograde amnesia).
regions.approx_location: Curved structure in the medial temporal lobe, bilateral.
regions.famous_case_or_evidence: Patient H.M. (Henry Molaison), after bilateral medial temporal lobectomy in 1953 for epilepsy, became severely amnesic — the foundational case (studied by Brenda Milner, later Suzanne Corkin) for localizing declarative memory formation to the hippocampus.

regions.name: Striatum (Caudate + Putamen)
regions.one_liner: Input hub of the basal ganglia; learns which actions/habits to select based on reward history.
functions: Receiving dopaminergic input signaling reward prediction error
regions.lesion_effects: Progressive degeneration (especially of the caudate) causes Huntington's disease — involuntary jerky movements (chorea), cognitive decline and personality change.
regions.approx_location: Caudate (arcs around the thalamus) and putamen, deep subcortical, lateral to the thalamus.

regions.name: Globus Pallidus (GPe/GPi)
regions.one_liner: Output gate of the basal ganglia; its internal segment tonically inhibits the thalamus to suppress unwanted movement until released.
functions: External segment (GPe) relays the indirect pathway to the subthalamic nucleus
Internal segment (GPi) is a major basal-ganglia output nucleus inhibiting the thalamus
regions.lesion_effects: GPi is a common deep-brain-stimulation target for Parkinson's disease and dystonia; pathological damage here can disturb movement initiation and cause abnormal postures, while therapeutic lesioning/stimulation can relieve rigidity.
regions.approx_location: Medial to the putamen, deep subcortical, split into external (GPe) and internal (GPi) segments.

regions.name: Subthalamic Nucleus (STN)
regions.one_liner: Small but powerful 'brake' in the indirect pathway that excites output nuclei to suppress competing movements.
functions: Excitatory driver of GPi/SNr output (indirect and 'hyperdirect' pathways)
Action-selection braking to prevent premature or competing movements
regions.lesion_effects: Damage causes hemiballismus — violent, involuntary flinging movements of the contralateral limbs; the STN is also the most common deep-brain-stimulation target for Parkinson's disease, where stimulation improves motor symptoms but can sometimes increase impulsivity.
regions.approx_location: Small lens-shaped nucleus just below the thalamus, adjacent to the substantia nigra.

regions.name: Nucleus Accumbens
regions.one_liner: Core of the brain's reward circuit — translates motivation and pleasure signals into approach behavior.
functions: Integrating limbic input (amygdala/hippocampus) with dopaminergic (VTA) signals
regions.lesion_effects: Central to addiction: drugs of abuse hijack this dopamine-driven circuit; animal lesion/inactivation studies show reduced motivation for both natural and drug rewards and reduced cue-triggered 'wanting' behavior.
regions.approx_location: Ventral striatum, below the caudate/putamen junction.

regions.name: Ventral Tegmental Area (VTA)
regions.one_liner: Major dopamine source signaling reward prediction and driving motivation and reinforcement learning.
functions: Dopaminergic reward-prediction-error signaling (phasic bursts for better-than-expected outcomes)
Projecting to nucleus accumbens/PFC (mesolimbic and mesocortical pathways)
regions.lesion_effects: Damage/dysfunction reduces motivation and reward-driven learning; VTA dysfunction is implicated in addiction and studied in depression (anhedonia), mostly via animal lesion/optogenetic work rather than clean human lesion cases.
regions.approx_location: Ventral midbrain, near the substantia nigra.

regions.name: Substantia Nigra (pars compacta)
regions.one_liner: Dopamine source for the motor loop; its loss is the hallmark of Parkinson's disease.
functions: Dopaminergic modulation of the striatum (nigrostriatal pathway)
Facilitating the direct pathway / suppressing the indirect pathway to enable movement
regions.lesion_effects: Progressive loss of these dopaminergic neurons causes Parkinson's disease: bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor and postural instability — symptoms typically appear only after roughly 50-80% of these neurons are already lost.
regions.approx_location: Midbrain, dorsal to the cerebral peduncles; pars compacta is the pigmented, dopamine-producing part.

regions.name: Cerebellum
regions.one_liner: Fine-tunes movement timing and accuracy, and calibrates motor learning through error correction.
functions: Error-based motor learning/calibration using sensory feedback
Contributes to some cognitive and timing tasks
regions.lesion_effects: Causes ataxia (uncoordinated movement), dysmetria (over/undershooting targets), intention tremor, and impaired motor adaptation (e.g., poor adjustment to prism-shifted vision or novel force fields), while raw muscle strength remains normal.
regions.approx_location: Posterior fossa, below the occipital lobe, dorsal to the brainstem.

regions.name: Locus Coeruleus
regions.one_liner: The brain's primary noradrenaline source; drives arousal, vigilance and response to novelty/stress.
functions: Noradrenergic modulation of arousal and alertness
Phasic firing tied to attention/orienting toward salient or novel stimuli
Modulating cortical signal-to-noise ratio during stress
regions.lesion_effects: Locus coeruleus neurons are among the earliest to degenerate in both Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, often before hallmark pathology appears in cortex/substantia nigra; loss is linked to disrupted arousal, attention and sleep regulation.
regions.approx_location: Small nucleus in the dorsal pons, near the fourth ventricle, bilateral.

regions.name: Raphe Nuclei
regions.one_liner: Chain of midline nuclei and the brain's main serotonin source, shaping mood, sleep and impulse control.
functions: Serotonergic modulation of mood and anxiety
Regulating sleep-wake architecture (contributes to REM sleep regulation)
regions.lesion_effects: Dysfunction is strongly associated with depression and anxiety (the target of SSRIs, which block serotonin reuptake); animal lesion studies show disrupted sleep architecture and increased impulsive/aggressive behavior, though clean human lesion evidence is rare since damage is seldom isolated to the raphe alone.
regions.approx_location: Midline of the brainstem, spanning midbrain to medulla (e.g., the dorsal raphe nucleus in the midbrain).

pathways.title: Recognizing a Face
pathways.scenario_sentence: You glance across a crowded room and instantly recognize a friend's face.

steps.what_happens: Light patterns from the face reach the retina and are relayed via the thalamus (LGN) to primary visual cortex, where basic edges, contrast and orientation are extracted in a retinotopic map.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the first cortical stage of 'seeing' anything — without intact V1, no conscious visual image of the face can form.
steps.evidence_or_method: Human visual evoked potential (C1 component) and macaque LGN/V1 latencies (~20-30ms onset in monkeys; longer human conduction distance implies ~50-70ms).

steps.what_happens: Ventral-stream area V4 refines color and mid-level shape/contour information, beginning to separate the face's form from the background.
steps.why_it_matters: Builds the shape/color scaffolding that face-specific processing depends on.
steps.evidence_or_method: Macaque V4 shape/color-tuned single-unit response timing; precise human latency is inferred, not directly measured non-invasively.

steps.what_happens: The fusiform face area performs fast, holistic structural encoding of the face, distinguishing it from other object categories.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the brain's dedicated specialization for face shape — damage here causes prosopagnosia even with otherwise normal vision.
steps.evidence_or_method: N170 ERP component (occipito-temporal electrodes), source-localized to the fusiform gyrus/FFA (Gao et al., 2019, Psychophysiology).

steps.what_happens: The specific facial identity is matched against stored memories in the medial temporal lobe/hippocampus while the amygdala tags any emotional significance.
steps.why_it_matters: Recognizing THAT something is a face and recognizing WHO it is are separable steps that can be selectively impaired independently.
steps.evidence_or_method: fMRI studies of familiar-face recognition implicate medial-temporal/hippocampal regions; timing is estimated from MEG/intracranial familiarity effects rather than one sharp ERP marker.

steps.what_happens: Prefrontal regions integrate identity and emotional tag into a conscious, nameable recognition ('that's my friend Alex').
steps.why_it_matters: This step converts a visual/memory match into a usable, reportable social recognition.
steps.evidence_or_method: fMRI/EEG studies of person-identification implicate prefrontal integration; this final stage is the least precisely time-locked step in the sequence.

pathways.accuracy_caveats: Millisecond values are approximate averages from group-level EEG/MEG/fMRI studies using simplified lab tasks, not measurements of a single real-world glance. The N170 (step 3) indexes detecting face-like structure, not full personal-identity recognition, which likely takes longer and is less precisely time-locked (steps 4-5 are estimates, not established ERP components).

pathways.title: Recalling a Word or Name
pathways.scenario_sentence: You try to remember the name of an old classmate.

steps.what_happens: A retrieval cue ('what was her name?') triggers a strategic search, coordinated by prefrontal and parietal executive regions.
steps.why_it_matters: Retrieval is an active search process that can succeed, fail, or stall — as in the 'tip-of-the-tongue' state.
steps.evidence_or_method: fMRI studies of directed memory search show dorsolateral prefrontal and parietal engagement during retrieval effort.

steps.what_happens: The hippocampus performs 'pattern completion' — using a partial cue to reactivate the full memory trace distributed across cortex.
steps.why_it_matters: This computation lets a small hint (a face, a context) unlock a whole memory.
steps.evidence_or_method: Computational memory models (Marr, 1971; O'Reilly & McClelland, 1994) and hippocampal lesion/imaging studies; exact human timing is inferred from ERP 'old/new' effects, not measured directly for this specific computation.

steps.what_happens: A frontally-generated 'familiarity' signal can arise ('I know this person') even before full recollection occurs.
steps.why_it_matters: Familiarity and full recollection are dissociable memory processes with different reliability.
steps.evidence_or_method: Frontal/early old-new ERP effect associated with familiarity, roughly 300-500ms post-cue (Rugg & Curran, 2007 review).

steps.what_happens: If retrieval succeeds, a later parietal signal reflects full recollection — recovering specific contextual detail.
steps.why_it_matters: Distinguishes vague familiarity from rich, detailed remembering, explaining why some memories 'come back in a flash' with context and others stay vague.
steps.evidence_or_method: Parietal old/new ERP effect, roughly 500-800ms post-cue, associated with recollection (Rugg & Curran, 2007).

steps.what_happens: Once the concept is retrieved, language areas convert it into the specific word/name and prepare it for speech output.
steps.why_it_matters: This lexical-retrieval step is exactly where 'tip-of-the-tongue' failures happen — the concept/face can be known without accessing its word form.
steps.evidence_or_method: Tip-of-the-tongue research (Brown & McNeill, 1966) and neuroimaging implicating left insula/frontal regions in successful word-form retrieval.

pathways.accuracy_caveats: Most memory-retrieval timing here comes from group-averaged ERP 'old/new' effects, not sharp single events — the numbers mark typical windows, not fixed checkpoints, and vary enormously with how well-learned the memory is and how strong the retrieval cue is.

pathways.title: Fear Response to a Sudden Threat
pathways.scenario_sentence: You spot what might be a snake on the path in front of you.

steps.what_happens: A crude, low-resolution version of the scene is relayed through the thalamus toward the amygdala via a fast subcortical shortcut, in parallel with the slower cortical route.
steps.why_it_matters: This 'quick and dirty' route can trigger a protective reaction before you've consciously identified what you saw.
steps.evidence_or_method: MEG gamma-synchronization study reporting thalamic/hypothalamic activity ~10-20ms and amygdala activity by ~20-30ms post-stimulus (Luo et al., 2007, PNAS); direct human tract-tracing evidence for a monosynaptic thalamo-amygdala route is more limited than in rodents — treat this pathway's speed in humans as an active research question.

steps.what_happens: The amygdala performs rapid threat evaluation on the coarse input (shape, low spatial-frequency contrast) and can begin triggering a defensive response.
steps.why_it_matters: This speed advantage — acting before full visual analysis finishes — is thought to be adaptive: better a false alarm than a fatal delay.
steps.evidence_or_method: Human intracranial amygdala recordings show responses to fearful faces beginning ~74-88ms post-stimulus (Méndez-Bértolo et al., 2016, Nature Neuroscience).

steps.what_happens: The amygdala engages the hypothalamus, which triggers the sympathetic 'fight-or-flight' cascade — stress hormones and bodily readiness (heart rate, blood flow to muscles).
steps.why_it_matters: This converts a brain signal into the felt bodily experience of fear before you've consciously decided how to react.
steps.evidence_or_method: Amygdala-hypothalamic-brainstem fear circuitry established mainly in animal lesion/stimulation studies (LeDoux and colleagues); precise human millisecond timing for this autonomic cascade is not directly measurable non-invasively and is estimated here.

steps.what_happens: In parallel, the slower, detailed cortical ('high road') visual pathway finishes analyzing the object properly — is it really a snake, or a curved stick?
steps.why_it_matters: This slower but more accurate pathway can override or confirm the fast amygdala-driven alarm.
steps.evidence_or_method: Standard visual object-recognition timing; full object categorization ERP effects typically emerge ~150-250ms.

steps.what_happens: The ventromedial prefrontal cortex evaluates the detailed information and, if the 'threat' is harmless, helps down-regulate the amygdala, while the insula and ACC register bodily sensations and any conflict.
steps.why_it_matters: This regulation step is impaired in some anxiety disorders — an overactive amygdala without adequate prefrontal 'braking' can produce persistent or excessive fear.
steps.evidence_or_method: vmPFC-amygdala functional connectivity and its role in fear regulation/extinction is documented in human fMRI (e.g., Phelps et al., 2004, Neuron), though exact millisecond timing of this regulatory step is not precisely established.

pathways.accuracy_caveats: The 'fast subcortical low road vs. slow cortical high road' dual-pathway model for fear was built primarily on rodent tract-tracing (LeDoux); in humans it is inferred from EEG/MEG/intracranial timing and remains debated (some researchers argue the human low road is weaker or less direct than in rodents). Hypothalamic/autonomic-step timings are extrapolated from general fear-circuit knowledge, not directly timed non-invasively in humans.

pathways.title: Making a Decision
pathways.scenario_sentence: You're deciding between two snacks at a vending machine.

steps.what_happens: Visual information about both options is processed and spatial attention is allocated to compare them.
steps.why_it_matters: You can't weigh options you haven't perceptually registered — attention determines what enters the decision process.
steps.evidence_or_method: Standard visual latency (V1 ~50-70ms) plus parietal attention engagement.

steps.what_happens: The ventromedial prefrontal/orbitofrontal cortex assigns a subjective value to each option, incorporating past experience and current state (e.g., hunger).
steps.why_it_matters: This 'common currency' computation lets you compare completely different things (candy vs. chips) on one internal value scale.
steps.evidence_or_method: Single-neuron recordings in macaque OFC encoding relative subjective value (Padoa-Schioppa & Assad, 2006, Nature) and human fMRI value-correlate studies (Rangel and colleagues).

steps.what_happens: Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex holds the options and values in working memory while the anterior cingulate cortex monitors for conflict if the values are close.
steps.why_it_matters: Close-call decisions take measurably longer and engage more conflict-monitoring activity — why difficult decisions feel effortful.
steps.evidence_or_method: ACC conflict-monitoring literature (Botvinick et al., 2001) and P300 latency increasing with decision difficulty.

steps.what_happens: Evidence for each option accumulates (a drift-diffusion-like process) until one option crosses a decision threshold, involving striatal and parietal circuits.
steps.why_it_matters: Explains the classic speed-accuracy tradeoff: rushing lowers the threshold and raises errors; deliberation raises accuracy at the cost of time.
steps.evidence_or_method: Centro-parietal positivity ('CPP') tracks evidence accumulation to threshold, roughly 250-500ms depending on difficulty (O'Connell et al., 2012, Nature Neuroscience); drift-diffusion modeling (Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008).

steps.what_happens: Once threshold is crossed, primary motor cortex executes the chosen action (reaching for the snack).
steps.why_it_matters: This is the irreversible commitment point — before this, the 'decision' is still internally revisable.
steps.evidence_or_method: Motor-evoked potential and reaction-time studies linking decision commitment to movement onset.

pathways.accuracy_caveats: These figures describe simple, well-studied lab decisions (two-alternative forced-choice tasks); real-world decisions with more options, social context, or higher stakes take much longer, and the exact millisecond figures shift substantially with decision difficulty and confidence.

pathways.title: Reading a Sentence
pathways.scenario_sentence: You read the sentence: 'The tired cat sat on the...' and predict what comes next.

steps.what_happens: Visual cortex registers the basic shapes of the printed letters.
steps.why_it_matters: Reading starts as pure vision, before any letter or word knowledge is applied.
steps.evidence_or_method: Standard V1 visual evoked potential latency.

steps.what_happens: A specialized patch of the fusiform gyrus (the 'visual word form area', adjacent to face-processing cortex) recognizes the letter string as a familiar written word shape, independent of font or case.
steps.why_it_matters: This is why skilled readers recognize whole familiar words almost instantly rather than sounding out every letter.
steps.evidence_or_method: Visual word form area studies (Dehaene & Cohen, 2011, Trends in Cognitive Sciences) report word-selective responses in a ~150-200ms window, in a region adjacent to but distinct from the face-selective N170 source.

steps.what_happens: Wernicke's area and surrounding temporal/semantic regions access the word's meaning; an unexpected next word ('...on the moon' instead of '...on the mat') produces a distinctive brain signature.
steps.why_it_matters: Shows the brain actively predicts upcoming words from context rather than processing them in isolation.
steps.evidence_or_method: N400 ERP component, peaking ~400ms, larger for semantically unexpected words (Kutas & Hillyard, 1980, Science).

steps.what_happens: Broca's area parses the sentence's grammatical structure and, if reading aloud, prepares the articulatory motor plan.
steps.why_it_matters: Grammar processing and speech planning are separable from word meaning — why Broca's aphasia patients understand meaning but struggle to produce fluent, grammatical sentences.
steps.evidence_or_method: Syntactic ERP effects (e.g., P600, linked to grammatical reanalysis) and classic Broca's-aphasia lesion-symptom mapping.

steps.what_happens: If reading aloud, primary motor cortex (orofacial region) executes the speech articulation.
steps.why_it_matters: Converts the linguistic plan into physical sound.
steps.evidence_or_method: Standard motor execution timing following articulatory planning.

pathways.accuracy_caveats: This describes one influential (broadly dual-route-inspired) sequence; real reading also uses a parallel phonological route via parietal/temporal regions for unfamiliar or nonsense words, and skilled silent reading can overlap or shortcut several stages rather than running them strictly in series.

pathways.title: Learning a New Motor Skill
pathways.scenario_sentence: You practice a new tennis serve over several training sessions.

steps.what_happens: Early attempts are slow and effortful — prefrontal and parietal executive regions are heavily engaged to consciously control each part of the movement.
steps.why_it_matters: Explains why a brand-new skill feels mentally exhausting even though the movements themselves are simple — you're using effortful general-purpose control, not a specialized motor circuit yet.
steps.evidence_or_method: Doyon et al. (2003, 2018) models of motor sequence learning describe an early 'fast learning' stage with strong prefrontal/associative involvement.

steps.what_happens: With each attempt, the cerebellum compares the predicted sensory outcome (an internal 'forward model') against what actually happened, computing an error signal to adjust the next attempt.
steps.why_it_matters: This trial-by-trial error correction is the core mechanism of motor learning — why immediate feedback speeds learning dramatically.
steps.evidence_or_method: Cerebellar internal/forward-model theory of motor learning (Wolpert, Miall & Kawato, 1998, Trends in Cognitive Sciences).

steps.what_happens: As the sequence becomes more reliable, control shifts toward the basal ganglia (striatum), which increasingly encodes the whole sequence as one learned 'chunk'.
steps.why_it_matters: This chunking is why a practiced serve eventually feels like one smooth motion rather than separate decisions.
steps.evidence_or_method: Striatal associative-to-sensorimotor shift with automaticity, and action-sequence chunking (Yin & Knowlton, 2006, Nature Reviews Neuroscience; Graybiel, 1998).

steps.what_happens: Dopaminergic signals from the substantia nigra reinforce successful movement patterns, strengthening the corticostriatal connections that produced a good outcome.
steps.why_it_matters: This reward-based strengthening is why skills improve faster with clear success/failure feedback.
steps.evidence_or_method: Nigrostriatal dopamine's role in reinforcement learning and corticostriatal plasticity (Schultz, 1998, and later studies).

steps.what_happens: With enough practice, the skill becomes largely automatic ('procedural memory') — executable with minimal conscious prefrontal involvement.
steps.why_it_matters: Procedural memories are famously robust — they survive even severe declarative-memory damage, showing they are stored differently from facts and events.
steps.evidence_or_method: Amnesic patient H.M. learned and retained new motor skills (e.g., mirror-tracing) at a normal rate despite no explicit memory of practicing them (Milner, 1962; Corkin, 1968).

pathways.accuracy_caveats: Motor skill learning unfolds over minutes, sessions and days/weeks, not milliseconds. The approx_ms values above are a SCHEMATIC animation timeline only (relative order/spacing within a compressed practice montage), not measured neural latencies — treat this pathway's timing as ORDER of engagement, not literal figures. The Doyon fast/slow-stage model and cortical-to-subcortical shift are broadly supported but simplified here; real circuits overlap throughout learning rather than handing off cleanly.

pathways.title: Shifting Attention to a Sudden Event
pathways.scenario_sentence: While driving, a ball suddenly rolls into the street ahead of you.

steps.what_happens: The sudden motion and contrast change registers in visual cortex as a salient, bottom-up event.
steps.why_it_matters: Sudden, high-contrast, moving stimuli automatically grab visual processing resources before you consciously 'decide' to look.
steps.evidence_or_method: Standard early visual response latency (V1 ~50-70ms); subcortical salience circuits (superior colliculus/pulvinar, not separately modeled here) also contribute to this capture.

steps.what_happens: MT/V5 rapidly computes the object's motion direction and speed.
steps.why_it_matters: Fast motion computation is essential for predicting where a moving hazard will be a moment from now, not just where it is.
steps.evidence_or_method: MT/V5 motion-selective response latencies in primate electrophysiology, generally in the 80-120ms range.

steps.what_happens: Attention is captured and reoriented toward the ball's location, visible as a lateralized attention signal over posterior scalp contralateral to the object.
steps.why_it_matters: This attention 'grab' is largely automatic and hard to suppress — it lets us react to sudden hazards even while focused on something else.
steps.evidence_or_method: N2pc ERP component (attention-related lateralized negativity), peaking roughly 200-250ms post-onset (Eimer, 1996; Luck & Hillyard, 1994).

steps.what_happens: The locus coeruleus fires a phasic burst of noradrenaline in response to the salient event, boosting the gain/responsiveness of relevant cortical circuits brain-wide.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the neural basis of the sudden 'jolt' of alertness — a brief, brain-wide shift into a more vigilant mode.
steps.evidence_or_method: Adaptive gain theory linking phasic locus coeruleus activity to attention/orienting and the P300 component (Aston-Jones & Cohen, 2005, Annual Review of Neuroscience) — based largely on animal electrophysiology, with human evidence more indirect (pupil dilation, fMRI proxies).

steps.what_happens: The anterior cingulate cortex helps override the ongoing action if needed, and motor cortex executes the corrective response (braking).
steps.why_it_matters: This conflict-resolution/override step allows rapid, appropriate behavioral correction instead of continuing a now-inappropriate action.
steps.evidence_or_method: ACC's role in action monitoring/override in conflict paradigms (Botvinick et al., 2001); driving-simulator studies cite additional reaction-time cost above pure perceptual latency for braking responses.

pathways.accuracy_caveats: This pathway compresses a well-studied lab phenomenon (covert attentional capture in simple visual-search displays) onto a more complex real-world scenario (driving). Real hazard-braking reaction times vary widely — commonly cited overall brake-reaction times in driving research are roughly 0.7-1.5 seconds, depending on expectancy, distraction and individual differences — so this region-by-region breakdown is illustrative, not a validated decomposition of real driving reaction time.

pathways.title: Sleep and Memory Consolidation
pathways.scenario_sentence: You study for an exam in the evening, sleep, and remember the material better the next morning.

steps.what_happens: During studying (while awake), the hippocampus rapidly encodes new episodic memory traces, acting as a 'fast learner' that can bind new information in a single exposure.
steps.why_it_matters: This fast-binding capacity lets you learn new facts in minutes, but these fresh traces are initially fragile and hippocampus-dependent.
steps.evidence_or_method: Complementary Learning Systems theory (McClelland, McNaughton & O'Reilly, 1995) — hippocampus as fast learner vs. neocortex as slow learner.

steps.what_happens: Entering NREM slow-wave sleep, the thalamus generates sleep spindles (brief ~12-15Hz oscillation bursts) that help gate out sensory input and coordinate cortical activity.
steps.why_it_matters: Spindles are believed to open a temporal window that helps synchronize cortical and hippocampal activity for memory transfer.
steps.evidence_or_method: Sleep spindle-memory correlations reviewed in Diekelmann & Born (2010, Nature Reviews Neuroscience).

steps.what_happens: The hippocampus generates sharp-wave ripples — brief (~50-100ms), fast (~150-250Hz) oscillatory bursts during which recently learned activity patterns are 'replayed' in compressed, accelerated form.
steps.why_it_matters: This replay is thought to be the literal mechanism by which the day's experiences get rehearsed for storage — a fast-forwarded highlight reel played to the rest of the brain.
steps.evidence_or_method: Hippocampal sharp-wave ripple replay during sleep, extensively documented in rodents (Wilson & McNaughton, 1994, Science), with converging human intracranial/fMRI evidence.

steps.what_happens: Hippocampal ripples become temporally coupled with cortical slow oscillations (~0.5-1Hz) and thalamic spindles, forming coordinated 'triple coupling' thought to time information transfer to cortex.
steps.why_it_matters: The precision of this coupling (ripples nested in spindles nested in slow-oscillation up-states) predicts overnight retention in some studies.
steps.evidence_or_method: Slow oscillation-spindle-ripple coupling literature (Staresina et al., 2015, Nature Neuroscience).

steps.what_happens: Over repeated replay across the night (and following nights), the memory trace becomes gradually distributed across neocortical networks, including prefrontal and parietal regions, and less dependent on the hippocampus.
steps.why_it_matters: This 'systems consolidation' explains why old memories can survive hippocampal damage (as in H.M.), while very recent memories cannot.
steps.evidence_or_method: Systems consolidation theory and temporally graded retrograde amnesia in hippocampal amnesia patients (Squire & Alvarez, 1995); whether cortex ever becomes fully hippocampus-independent remains debated (multiple trace theory offers a competing account).

pathways.accuracy_caveats: All approx_ms values in this pathway are SCHEMATIC (representing order and relative spacing within a compressed overnight animation), not real elapsed times — consolidation actually unfolds over multiple sleep cycles across a full night and further nights. The specific causal role of REM sleep (versus NREM/slow-wave sleep) in consolidation remains actively debated and is deliberately not included as a distinct step here. 'Systems consolidation' is a leading model, but multiple trace theory and trace transformation theory offer competing accounts of how completely and quickly hippocampal dependence is lost.

glossary.plain_definition: The basic signaling cell of the brain; receives, processes and passes on electrical/chemical signals.
The tiny gap where one neuron passes a chemical signal to the next.
The brief electrical spike a neuron fires when it 'sends a message' down its length.
A chemical messenger released at a synapse that excites or inhibits the next neuron.
A neurotransmitter central to motivation, reward-prediction and movement — not simply 'the pleasure chemical'.
A neurotransmitter involved in mood, sleep and impulse control; target of common antidepressants (SSRIs).
A neurotransmitter driving arousal, alertness and the stress/fight-or-flight response.
Glutamate is the brain's main 'go' signal between neurons; GABA is the main 'stop/quiet down' signal — together they balance brain activity.
The cortex is the folded outer layer doing most higher-level processing; 'subcortical' structures sit beneath it handling emotion, memory, movement and basic drives.
A gyrus is a raised fold on the brain's surface; a sulcus is a groove between folds — together they let a lot of cortex fit in a small skull.
Gray matter is mostly neuron cell bodies (where processing happens); white matter is the myelinated 'wiring' carrying signals between regions.
A fatty insulating sheath around axons that speeds up electrical signal transmission.
The tendency for some functions (e.g., language, typically left-sided) to rely more on one brain hemisphere than the other — a matter of degree, not an absolute split.
The distorted 'body map' in motor and somatosensory cortex, where sensitive/dexterous body parts (lips, hands) get disproportionately more cortical space.
An organization in visual cortex where neighboring points in the visual field are processed by neighboring cortical neurons.
An organization in auditory cortex where different sound frequencies are mapped to different cortical locations.
The specific stimulus (e.g., patch of visual space, sound frequency) that makes a given neuron respond.
The brain's ability to physically reorganize — strengthening, weakening, or rewiring connections — in response to experience.
A lasting strengthening of the connection between two neurons after repeated co-activation; a leading cellular model of how memories are stored.
The mismatch between an expected and actual reward, signaled by dopamine bursts (better than expected) or dips (worse than expected); drives reinforcement learning.
The mental 'scratchpad' that holds and manipulates a small amount of information for seconds while you use it.
Umbrella term for planning, inhibition, flexibility and goal-directed control, largely supported by prefrontal cortex.
Memory for facts and events that can be consciously recalled and stated ('I remember that...').
Memory for skills and habits (e.g., riding a bike) that operates largely without conscious recall.
The gradual process by which memories shift from depending on the hippocampus to being stored more independently in the neocortex, thought to occur especially during sleep.
A research pattern where damage to region A impairs task 1 but not task 2, while damage to region B does the opposite — strong evidence the two functions are separable.
Research inferring a brain region's function by studying what ability is lost when that region is damaged (by injury, stroke, surgery or disease).
A method that records electrical brain activity via scalp electrodes; excellent timing precision (milliseconds) but coarse spatial detail.
A small EEG voltage pattern time-locked to a specific event (like seeing a face), extracted by averaging many trials.
Functional MRI infers brain activity from blood-oxygenation changes (BOLD signal); great spatial detail but a slow, several-second lag behind actual neural firing.
A method recording tiny magnetic fields from brain activity; combines EEG-like millisecond timing with somewhat better spatial localization.
An ERP brain-wave dip around 130-200ms after seeing a face, linked to fast structural face processing in the fusiform gyrus.
An ERP brain-wave dip peaking around 400ms when a word doesn't fit the meaning of its sentence context.
A positive ERP brain-wave peak around 300-500ms linked to detecting a significant or decision-relevant event.
An ERP signature (~200-250ms) showing that visual attention has shifted toward a target on one side of space.
A slow buildup of brain activity, starting hundreds of milliseconds before a voluntary movement, famously studied by Benjamin Libet in debates about free will.
A brief, fast burst of hippocampal activity during rest/sleep thought to 'replay' recent experiences to help consolidate them into long-term memory.
A short burst of 12-15Hz brain-wave activity generated by the thalamus during NREM sleep, linked to memory consolidation.
NREM (non-rapid-eye-movement) sleep includes deep slow-wave sleep linked to memory replay; REM sleep is the dream-rich stage with brain activity resembling wakefulness.
The hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal signaling chain that releases stress hormones (like cortisol) in response to threat, initiated largely by the hypothalamus.

accuracy_pitfalls: The '10% of the brain' myth is false — brain imaging shows nearly all regions are active over the course of a day, just not all firing at maximum simultaneously.

'Left-brained vs. right-brained' personality typing is an oversimplification; real hemispheric lateralization (e.g., language usually left, spatial attention often right-weighted) is a matter of statistical bias, not a hard 'logical vs. creative' personality split.

fMRI 'activation' should not be read as 'this region does X and only X' — BOLD signal is an indirect, several-second-delayed proxy for neural activity, and most regions participate in multiple functions/networks rather than being single-purpose modules.

The amygdala is often oversold as 'the fear center' — it is central to threat/salience detection broadly (including some positive learning), and fear itself involves distributed circuitry (hypothalamus, periaqueductal gray, insula, cortex), not one nucleus alone.

LeDoux's thalamus-to-amygdala 'low road' for ultra-fast fear responses is well established in rodents via direct tract-tracing; in humans it is inferred mainly from MEG/EEG/intracranial timing, so present the human pathway and its exact latency as an active research question, not settled fact.

Avoid phrenology-style 'one bump/one region = one fixed faculty' framing — modern neuroscience emphasizes distributed networks; a labeled region is a major hub/contributor, not an exclusive seat of a mental faculty.

Libet's readiness-potential findings are commonly overinterpreted as 'proof free will is an illusion' — this remains a contested methodological and philosophical debate (e.g., whether the potential reflects the specific decision or a general readiness/threshold-crossing), and should be presented as an interesting, contested finding rather than settled fact.

The classic basal ganglia direct/indirect pathway diagram is a useful simplification, not the full picture — more recent research finds overlap and more nuanced roles (e.g., some 'indirect pathway' neurons also promote action) than the clean two-pathway model suggests.

Precise millisecond timings quoted for cognitive events (e.g., 'face recognition takes exactly 170ms') are group-averaged findings from specific lab paradigms with real inter-individual and inter-task variability — present them as typical/approximate windows, not fixed universal constants.
Memories are not stored like video recordings played back perfectly; they are reconstructive and can change slightly (or be distorted) each time they are recalled and 're-stored' (reconsolidation).

Dopamine is not simply the 'pleasure chemical' and serotonin deficiency is not a fully sufficient explanation for depression — the monoamine hypothesis of depression is now considered an incomplete oversimplification in current research; frame these neuromodulators in terms of their more specific, evidence-backed roles (reward prediction/motivational salience for dopamine; mood/sleep/impulse regulation for serotonin).

Language lateralization percentages (e.g., ~95-99% left-hemisphere dominance in right-handers) should not be presented as universal — left-handers and some right-handers show right-hemisphere or bilateral language dominance.

Motor/procedural skill learning is better described as a shift in the relative weighting of a distributed cortical-striatal-cerebellar network with practice, not a literal relocation of a skill from one brain area to another.

threejs_cdn.notes: cdnjs.cloudflare.com mirrors ONLY the core build files (three.module.js / three.min.js per revision) — confirmed via api.cdnjs.com/libraries/three.js, which lists no examples/jsm or addons directory at all. So OrbitControls/EffectComposer/RenderPass/UnrealBloomPass CANNOT come from cdnjs. They must come from cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@<version>/examples/jsm/..., which is jsdelivr's generic npm-package proxy (allowed under the 'cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/' rule) and serves the full published package tree, including the examples/jsm addons and three's package.json export map ('three/addons/*' -> './examples/jsm/*', confirmed by fetching the package.json). Recommendation: source BOTH the core module and every addon from jsdelivr's npm proxy at the SAME pinned version — never mix cdnjs-core with jsdelivr-addons, and never use an unpinned/latest path. All addon files import 'three' as a bare specifier (e.g. OrbitControls.js does `import {...} from 'three'`), which is exactly what the importmap above resolves. Versions 0.160.0 and 0.170.0 both have three.module.js as a single self-contained file; starting around 0.180.0, three.module.js began internally importing a sibling './three.core.js' via a relative path (still works fine via the CDN since jsdelivr serves the whole directory, but means the module is no longer a single portable text blob) — this is a good reason to always reference three.js via its CDN URL through the importmap rather than trying to inline/copy its source text. 0.170.0 is recommended as the newest version I could fully verify end-to-end (core + OrbitControls + EffectComposer + RenderPass + Pass + the Addons.js barrel confirming all four requested exports) without the file-split behavior of later versions.
