brain_model_options.name: Neuro.Wiki 3D Brain Atlas (CIT168 + DKT31 cortical parcellation)
brain_model_options.license: Mixed: cortex (DKT31) is CC0 1.0; whole-brain/subcortical layers are CC BY-SA 4.0
brain_model_options.format: glTF (served to an interactive WebGL viewer)
brain_model_options.segments_list: 437 named structures across 12 systems (cortex, tracts, deep grey/subcortical nuclei, ventricles, brainstem, cerebellum, amygdala, thalamic nuclei, hypothalamic regions)
brain_model_options.verdict: NOT PRACTICAL. This is the closest match in scope/licensing but (1) there is no direct download link for the raw glTF files — only an interactive viewer, so the underlying per-structure meshes are not obtainable without scraping the live site, which is itself borderline given the CC BY-SA attribution/share-alike terms; (2) the site's own disclaimer states deep/subcortical structures are 'registered, not segmented — approximate to about 7mm', i.e. not true independent per-structure meshes but a shared reference volume; (3) CC BY-SA is a copyleft license — bundling it would arguably obligate the resulting single HTML file to also be released under CC BY-SA, which is a real constraint for a personal project. Not recommended as an asset source.

brain_model_options.name: NIH 3D Print Exchange – 'Subcortical Structures' (3DPX-001944, by Roman Kessler)
brain_model_options.segments_list: Bilateral hippocampus, amygdala, thalamus, nucleus accumbens, caudate, pallidum, putamen, and brainstem — but delivered as ONE combined STL, not separate files; the page states individual parts are only available 'on request'.
brain_model_options.verdict: NOT PRACTICAL. Right structures, wrong packaging and wrong license: NC (NonCommercial) and SA (ShareAlike) clauses make it legally awkward to bundle into any project that might ever be shared/published beyond pure personal use, and it isn't pre-segmented into individual clickable meshes anyway — it's a single fused STL requiring manual re-segmentation in Blender/MeshLab before it would even be usable as ~10 separate clickable objects.

brain_model_options.name: Z-Anatomy (Blender template, derived from BodyParts3D/Anatomography)
brain_model_options.format: Blender scene (.blend) with individually named mesh objects per structure; would need manual export to glTF per-object
brain_model_options.segments_list: Full-body atlas including nervous system layer with named brain substructures (built on BodyParts3D's FMA-labelled parts), but requires opening Blender, isolating the ~10 desired brain objects, decimating/cleaning them, and exporting a new lightweight glTF yourself — a real production step, not a drop-in file.
brain_model_options.verdict: POSSIBLE BUT NOT A QUICK WIN. Best license of the three real candidates (share-alike is manageable for a small personal educational artifact with attribution), and the source geometry genuinely has separate named subcortical meshes. But it requires a manual Blender pipeline (open scene, isolate ~10 objects, decimate to a low enough triangle budget, export minimal glTF, base64-encode) entirely outside the 'single HTML file, fetch-only-from-CDN' authoring loop — real effort with an uncertain final file size (source models were originally OBJ files 'too large for GitHub' at 100MB+ before conversion, so heavy decimation would be mandatory). Not recommended for a first prototype; worth revisiting only if the procedural approach later feels visually insufficient.

brain_model_options.name: BodyParts3D / Anatomography (Database Center for Life Science, Japan)
brain_model_options.format: STL (converted from original OBJ; originals were too large for GitHub, some 100MB+)
brain_model_options.segments_list: General whole-body FMA-indexed parts (skin, bones, organs); repository documentation does not surface dedicated subcortical brain structure files as a ready subset — it's the raw source Z-Anatomy was built from, not a curated brain-only package.
brain_model_options.verdict: NOT PRACTICAL as a direct source for this project — same underlying data as Z-Anatomy but even less curated for brain-only use, share-alike licensed, and originally oversized before conversion.

brain_model_options.name: Sketchfab brain/subcortical models (e.g. 'Brain with subcortical structures and tracts' by Tracy A, and the aherrler/ailame collections)
brain_model_options.license: Unclear/unverified per-model — page content did not surface a CC0/CC-BY tag, only a 'NoAI' flag; most Sketchfab anatomy models are under the platform's Standard (non-redistributable) license unless explicitly marked CC
brain_model_options.format: glTF/GLB (Sketchfab's native download format), but gated behind Sketchfab's own viewer/download flow
brain_model_options.segments_list: Described as color-coded separate components: caudate (green), thalamus (orange), hippocampus (yellow), amygdala (red), putamen (purple) — visually separated but license status not confirmed as CC0/CC-BY, and downloading requires visiting Sketchfab per-model (not automatable/verifiable at scale here).
brain_model_options.verdict: NOT PRACTICAL / DO NOT USE without manually verifying the exact license on each model page first. Even if a specific model turned out to be CC0, this class of resource is irrelevant here anyway: the sandbox's CSP explicitly forbids fetching any non-script resource from any host outside the CDN allowlist, and Sketchfab is not on that allowlist — so a Sketchfab-hosted GLB could only be used by manually downloading it once, converting/compressing it, and base64-embedding the bytes directly into the HTML (same effort/size problem as the Z-Anatomy path, with added license uncertainty on top).

brain_model_options.name: General conclusion on real assets
brain_model_options.verdict: No real free asset is directly practical for this project. The combination of requirements is unusually strict: (1) truly permissive license (CC0 or plain CC-BY, no NC/SA complications), (2) genuinely pre-segmented into ~10 separate meshes rather than one fused blob, (3) directly downloadable without a manual request/Blender pipeline, and (4) small enough that base64 (which inflates size ~33%) still fits comfortably under the 16MB total-page cap alongside all UI/JS/CSS. Every candidate found fails at least one of these, and most fail two or three. On top of that, the sandbox's own rules forbid loading any GLB via a live external fetch — even a perfect asset could only be used by hand-converting it to a base64 data URI baked into the file at authoring time (via GLTFLoader.parse(arrayBuffer) rather than loader.load(url)), never via loader.load() to a remote path. Given all this, the procedural approach (section C) is not a fallback — it is the correct primary path for this project.

tech.procedural_brain_recipe:
GOAL: an elegant, stylized-but-recognizable brain built entirely from Three.js primitives + noise displacement, with ~10 clickable subcortical structures, at 60fps on a laptop, single HTML file.

1) NOISE SOURCE
Use `simplex-noise` from jsdelivr's npm proxy for CPU-side vertex displacement (verified: https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/simplex-noise@4.0.3/dist/esm/simplex-noise.js, ESM, exports createNoise3D). Import it via the same importmap pattern: `"simplex-noise": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/simplex-noise@4.0.3/dist/esm/simplex-noise.js"`. Use `createNoise3D()` once (seeded) and sample it as fractal Brownian motion (fBm): sum 3-4 octaves, each doubling frequency and halving amplitude, e.g. `fbm(p) = Σ noise3D(p.x*f, p.y*f, p.z*f) * a` for f in [2,4,8,16], a in [1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.12], normalized. This is cheap enough to run once at mesh-build time (not per frame) since the cortex shape is static geometry, not GPU-animated.

2) CEREBRAL HEMISPHERES (the cortex "shell")
- Base geometry: `IcosahedronGeometry(radius, 5)` per hemisphere (20*4^5 = 20,480 triangles — enough vertex density for visible gyral folding without tanking triangle budget; avoid detail 6, which quadruples to ~82k triangles per hemisphere).
- Shape sculpting (before noise): non-uniformly scale each vertex position to turn the sphere into a brain-like ellipsoid — narrower medio-laterally, longer antero-posteriorly, and flatten the medial (inner) face toward x≈0 so the two hemispheres can sit flush against a longitudinal fissure. Add a smooth low-frequency "lobe mask" (a couple of smoothstep bumps as a function of the vertex's spherical angle) to bulge out a frontal pole, temporal lobe, and occipital pole, and taper the underside near where the brainstem attaches.
- Gyri/sulci: for every vertex, after the ellipsoid shaping, displace along the (pre-noise) vertex normal by `displacement = fbm(normalizedPosition * baseFrequency) * amplitude`, with amplitude roughly 3-6% of the hemisphere's mean radius. Use one lower-frequency fBm pass for the big, sweeping folds and blend in a smaller-amplitude higher-frequency pass for fine surface texture — this is what reads as "cortex" rather than "lumpy sphere."
- After displacing, call `geometry.computeVertexNormals()` so lighting responds correctly to the new folded surface.
- Longitudinal fissure: translate each hemisphere a small fixed distance away from the median plane (e.g. ±0.15 * radius along local X) so a visible groove/gap appears between them; optionally deepen it further by adding an extra localized noise term that only activates near x≈0 (a smoothstep falloff based on distance from the medial plane) to pull those vertices inward slightly, exaggerating the fissure.
- Material: default to a cheap "glassy" look — `MeshPhysicalMaterial({ transparent: true, opacity: 0.32, roughness: 0.35, metalness: 0, side: THREE.DoubleSide, depthWrite: false })` plus a subtle Fresnel rim-light added via `material.onBeforeCompile` (cheap, one extra dot-product term in the fragment shader). Offer real `transmission: 1, thickness: ...` (physically-based glass) as an optional "high quality" toggle, since transmission forces an extra background-capture render pass per transmissive object per frame and should be limited to at most the 2 hemisphere meshes if enabled at all.

3) CEREBELLUM
A separate, smaller ellipsoid (`IcosahedronGeometry` detail 4, or a scaled `SphereGeometry`) positioned posterior-inferior to the cerebral hemispheres. Give it a distinct "folia" texture instead of blobby gyri: combine a fine fBm with an added directional sine ripple, e.g. `displacement = fbm(p)*smallAmplitude + sin(localY * highFrequency) * rippleAmplitude`, so the ridges look parallel/laminar rather than random blobs — this single trick is what visually distinguishes cerebellum from cortex at a glance.

4) BRAINSTEM
A tapered, gently curved shape from `LatheGeometry` (rotate a hand-authored 2D profile — wider at the top for the midbrain, narrowing through pons and medulla) or a `CylinderGeometry` with different top/bottom radii as a cheaper approximation. Position it below the thalamus, angled slightly posterior, connecting the cerebrum to a short stub representing the spinal cord.

5) ~10 SUBCORTICAL STRUCTURES (clickable primitives)
Model each as the simplest primitive that reads as its real shape, positioned at approximate relative anatomical coordinates scaled to the model's own bounding box (not real MNI mm, just proportionally plausible placement), each as its own `THREE.Mesh` with `userData = { id, name, function, connections, lesionEffect, famousCase }`:
- Thalamus (paired ellipsoids, scaled spheres) — central, just above brainstem top.
- Hypothalamus (tiny sphere) — just below/anterior to thalamus.
- Hippocampus (paired) — a curved, C-shaped tube: define a `CatmullRomCurve3` with 4-5 control points tracing the classic "seahorse" curve, then `TubeGeometry(curve, ...)`; sits in the medial temporal lobe.
- Amygdala (paired) — small almond-shaped ellipsoid, anterior to each hippocampus.
- Caudate nucleus (paired) — a longer, gently arcing `TubeGeometry` along a curve sweeping over the thalamus (its real C-shape).
- Putamen (paired) — lens-shaped, a flattened/scaled sphere lateral to the globus pallidus.
- Globus pallidus (paired) — small wedge-shaped mesh (a scaled/cut sphere) medial to the putamen.
- Nucleus accumbens (paired) — tiny sphere at the head of the caudate/putamen junction, anteroventral.
- Corpus callosum — one flattened, curved `TubeGeometry` along a `CatmullRomCurve3` shaped like its real "C" profile (genu, body, splenium), arching over the thalamus, connecting the two hemispheres.
- (Brainstem and cerebellum, already built in steps 3-4, are also registered as clickable atlas entries using the same userData pattern, bringing the labelled-structure count to ~11-12.)

6) MAKING CORTICAL REGIONS (lobes) CLICKABLE — recommended hybrid approach
- Subcortical structures (step 5): trivial — they're already discrete meshes, so plain `raycaster.intersectObjects(subcorticalMeshes)` gives you the exact object and its userData directly.
- Cortical lobes on the folded hemisphere shell: rather than building 4-6 separate lobe meshes (seam-matching risk, since each would need to reproduce the exact same noise displacement at its boundary), tag every vertex of the single hemisphere geometry with a custom `Float32BufferAttribute('regionId', ...)` computed once at build time from each vertex's PRE-displacement spherical angle (theta/phi), using a small set of hand-tuned angular boundary rules approximating frontal/parietal/temporal/occipital/insula lobes (a lightweight "cortical parcellation by angle" lookup). On click: raycast against the single hemisphere mesh, take `intersection.face`, read the `regionId` attribute at its three vertex indices, and use a majority vote (or just vertex `a`) to resolve which lobe was hit, then look up that id in a name/function/connections table for the Atlas Explore panel. For the visual "selected region glows" effect, maintain a second attribute `highlightWeight` (0 or 1 per vertex, set for all vertices sharing the clicked regionId) and multiply it into emissive intensity inside a custom fragment shader (via `onBeforeCompile`) — this gives a clean per-region highlight with a single draw call and no extra geometry, and the shader-side highlight can be smoothly animated (lerp highlightWeight toward target) for a nice fade-in glow instead of an instant hard-edged selection.

7) LESION MODE
Since subcortical structures are discrete meshes, "lesioning" one is just toggling its visibility/opacity to near-zero (or replacing its material with a dim gray "damaged tissue" look) and showing the associated deficit text — no extra geometry work needed. For cortical lobes, reuse the same `regionId`/`highlightWeight` machinery to dim a lobe's opacity via a per-vertex attribute instead of a full separate mesh.

8) ACTIVATION-FLOW ANIMATION (for "Cognitive pathway journeys" mode)
Represent the traveling signal as a handful of small emissive spheres via a single `InstancedMesh` (not one Mesh per particle), moving each instance along a `CatmullRomCurve3` connecting the relevant structure centers for that scenario step, updating instance matrices in the render loop. Keep particle counts in the tens, not hundreds, per active step — this is a stylized diagram, not a real network simulation, so a handful of glowing dots plus a soft trailing line (e.g. a `Line2`/fat-line from `three/addons/lines/` or simply a `TubeGeometry` with an animated opacity gradient) communicates "activity flowing region to region" perfectly well.

9) NEURON POPULATION MODE (parametric simulation)
Keep this almost entirely OUT of the WebGL scene: implement a simple leaky-integrate-and-fire model in plain JS (no library needed — a few lines per neuron: `V += dt * (-(V - V_rest)/tau + I/C); if (V > V_thresh) { spike(); V = V_reset; }`), stepped with a fixed-timestep accumulator so it's independent of frame rate. Visualize the small population (e.g. 20-50 neurons) as an `InstancedMesh` of tiny spheres whose per-instance color/scale pulses on spike (updated via `setColorAt`/instance matrix, not per-instance Mesh objects). Draw the raster plot and membrane-potential trace on a plain 2D `<canvas>` overlay (not WebGL) — far cheaper and simpler than trying to plot in three.js, and it composites fine as an absolutely-positioned HTML element over the WebGL canvas.

10) PERFORMANCE BUDGET FOR 60FPS ON A LAPTOP
- Triangle budget: ~20-25k tris per hemisphere (detail-5 icosahedron) × 2, + a few thousand for cerebellum/brainstem, + a few hundred each for ~10-12 small subcortical primitives → comfortably under ~100-150k triangles total, well within a 60fps budget on integrated GPUs.
- Cap `renderer.setPixelRatio(Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio, 1.5))` — Retina/4K displays otherwise multiply fragment-shader cost 4x+, which matters a lot once bloom is added.
- `UnrealBloomPass` is the single most expensive part of the stack (multiple downsample+blur passes). Construct it at a reduced resolution (e.g. half the render target size) and/or gate it behind a "quality" toggle that's off by default on lower-end hardware (a simple heuristic: measure the first ~1s of actual frame times and auto-disable bloom/transmission if frame time exceeds ~20ms).
- Avoid shadow maps entirely — rely on emissive highlighting, rim lighting, and the translucent-material Fresnel trick instead of `castShadow`/`receiveShadow`, which are unnecessary for this stylized look and expensive to compute.
- Limit `MeshPhysicalMaterial({transmission:1})` usage to at most the 2 cortex-shell meshes if used at all — every transmissive surface triggers an extra render-to-texture pass of the background per frame.
- Use `InstancedMesh` for anything repeated (activation-flow particles, neuron population dots) rather than individual `Mesh` objects — each unique Mesh is a separate draw call, and draw-call count (not triangle count) is usually the real fps bottleneck on integrated GPUs.
- Do the noise-displacement geometry building ONCE at startup (bake it into the BufferGeometry), never per-frame — only material/shader uniforms and instance matrices should update in the render loop.
- If static/non-interactive decorative geometry is added later (e.g. a ventricle outline), merge it into as few draw calls as possible via `BufferGeometryUtils.mergeGeometries` (also available from `three/addons/utils/BufferGeometryUtils.js` on the same jsdelivr path).
single_file_constraints: cdnjs.cloudflare.com mirrors ONLY three.js's core build files per revision (three.module.js/three.min.js) — confirmed via api.cdnjs.com/libraries/three.js, which lists no examples/jsm or addons directory whatsoever. OrbitControls, EffectComposer, RenderPass, and UnrealBloomPass are only reachable through cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@<version>/examples/jsm/... — plan on jsdelivr as the sole source for both the core module AND every addon, at one pinned version, never mixed with cdnjs.

Always pin an exact three.js version in every CDN URL (e.g. @0.170.0), and use the IDENTICAL version string for the core module and every addon import. Three.js's internal APIs shift between revisions; loading OrbitControls from one revision against a three.module.js from another can produce subtle breakage (e.g. instanceof/class-identity checks failing) even when both files individually parse fine.

Starting around three@0.180.0, build/three.module.js stopped being a single self-contained file — it now does `import {...} from './three.core.js'` as a sibling file in the same directory. This is transparent when referencing the CDN URL directly (jsdelivr serves the whole directory), but means you can no longer treat three.module.js as one portable blob of text (e.g. don't try to inline/copy just its source) — always import it live via the importmap URL, don't vendor its source manually. This is a concrete reason 0.170.0 (still single-file) is a slightly safer pin than something newer if you ever want to reason about exactly what's being fetched.

Only a single <script type="importmap"> is allowed per document, and it must appear BEFORE any <script type="module"> that uses the bare specifiers it defines. Put it immediately after <head> opens, or right before your first module script.

Every addon file (OrbitControls.js, RenderPass.js, UnrealBloomPass.js, etc.) imports 'three' as a bare specifier internally — this only resolves correctly because the importmap maps the literal string 'three' to the exact module URL; if you ever rename that import key you break every addon silently.

The sandbox's CSP blocks ALL non-script fetches to any host outside the fonts.googleapis.com/gstatic.com pair — this means GLTFLoader.load(url) to any external .glb, any external texture image, and any external font JSON (for THREE.TextGeometry, which needs a FontLoader-fetched JSON) are all blocked outright. Any 3D text must be HTML/CSS overlay labels (plain absolutely-positioned divs synced to projected 3D coordinates, or three/addons/renderers/CSS2DRenderer.js) rather than TextGeometry — this is not optional, it's a hard CSP wall.

If a real GLB asset is ever added later (contra the recommendation below), it can only be used by base64-embedding its bytes directly in the HTML at authoring time and loading it via GLTFLoader.parse(arrayBuffer, ...) — never loader.load(url), since that would be a blocked external fetch even if pointed at an allowed CDN host (the allowlist permits script tags from those hosts, not arbitrary resource fetches).

Avoid Draco or KTX2 compressed glTF entirely if any real asset is ever embedded — their decoders are typically hosted on www.gstatic.com/draco/... or similar, which is not on the allowlist; there is no way to fetch the decoder wasm/js live, and inlining a whole Draco decoder's source into the page is a large, painful workaround for marginal size savings.

Base64 encoding inflates binary size by roughly 33% — factor this into the 16MB TOTAL page-size budget (HTML + all inline JS/CSS/data) if any binary asset is ever embedded; a nominally '4MB' GLB becomes ~5.3MB of base64 text, and also makes the file harder to read/edit.

cdn.tailwindcss.com's Play CDN script is a classic (non-module) script that scans the DOM's class attributes at runtime and injects a stylesheet — load it as a plain <script src=...> tag, separate from and independent of the importmap/module-script setup; it logs a 'not for production' console warning, which is expected and harmless for a prototype.

Opening the file directly via file:// works fine for the CDN-based ES module imports specifically BECAUSE they resolve to full https:// URLs through the importmap — this is a genuine cross-origin network fetch, which file:// pages are allowed to make (given proper CORS headers, which both cdnjs and jsdelivr send). What does NOT work under file:// is importing a SECOND local .js file via a relative path (e.g. import './app.js') — Chromium blocks that as a local-file CORS violation. This is a concrete, functional reason the whole app must live in one <script type="module"> block in one HTML file, not a preference.

file:// + CDN means the page is not truly 'fully offline' — it still needs live internet access to fetch three.js and its addons from jsdelivr on first load (and every reload, unless the browser's HTTP cache retains them). If a genuinely offline/air-gapped requirement ever surfaces, that is incompatible with the CDN-loading approach entirely and would require vendoring three.js source into the HTML file as inline text, which is a different (and much larger) design.

Disable shadow maps entirely (no castShadow/receiveShadow) — not just a performance nicety but avoids a class of subtle WebGL context/driver quirks on hybrid-GPU laptops; use emissive/rim lighting for the stylized look instead.

Add a minimal 'webglcontextlost'/'webglcontextrestored' listener pair — hybrid-GPU laptops (integrated+discrete switching) occasionally lose the WebGL context on tab visibility changes or GPU driver resets; a one-line guard that pauses the render loop and shows a 'tap to reload' message is cheap insurance for a demo the student might present live.

MeshPhysicalMaterial's transmission feature needs WebGL2 and a background render-target capture; verify renderer.capabilities.isWebGL2 and provide the plain-transparency fallback material path for older/weaker devices (notably some older Safari/iPad configurations) rather than assuming transmission always works.

The whole CDN allowlist (cdnjs, jsdelivr/npm, cdn.tailwindcss.com, code.jquery.com for SCRIPTS only, plus fonts.googleapis.com/gstatic.com for stylesheets/fonts) exactly matches the Claude Artifact sandbox's own CSP — worth confirming this project is specifically being built to run as/like a Claude Artifact, since that shapes which corners (external assets, fetch, workers) are permanently unavailable regardless of which real host eventually serves the file.
tech.recommendation:
Build this procedurally in Three.js — do not spend any more time searching for a real segmented brain asset. Every free option that has the right subcortical segmentation (Neuro.Wiki, NIH's 3DPX-001944, Z-Anatomy/BodyParts3D, assorted Sketchfab uploads) fails at least one hard requirement: a genuinely permissive license (several are CC BY-SA or CC BY-NC-SA, which are legally awkward to bundle into a shareable single-file artifact), true pre-segmentation into separate meshes rather than one fused blob, a direct no-manual-steps download, and a base64-safe size under the 16MB page cap. The sandbox's CSP compounds this: it blocks fetching any external GLB/texture/font outright, so even a perfect asset could only be used by hand-converting it to a base64 data URI at authoring time and loading it via GLTFLoader.parse() — real production effort for uncertain payoff, and it would leave the resulting HTML file bloated and hard to iterate on for a solo student project.

Concretely: pin Three.js r170 (https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.170.0/build/three.module.js) with all addons sourced from the same jsdelivr npm path (examples/jsm/...) via the importmap pattern verified above — never touch cdnjs for addons, since it only mirrors the core build. Build two IcosahedronGeometry(radius, 5) hemispheres sculpted into ellipsoids and displaced with 3-4 octave fBm noise (via simplex-noise@4.0.3 from jsdelivr) for gyri/sulci, a separate cerebellum mesh with a directional-ripple noise variant for its distinct "folia" look, a LatheGeometry/tapered-cylinder brainstem, and ~10-12 subcortical structures as simple primitives (spheres, TubeGeometry curves for hippocampus/caudate/corpus callosum) each carrying its own userData for the Atlas Explore panel. Make cortical lobes clickable via a per-vertex regionId attribute on the single hemisphere mesh (one draw call, clean raycasting, GPU-shader highlight glow) rather than separate lobe meshes, which would fight seam-matching against the shared noise field. Keep the whole scene under roughly 100-150k triangles, cap devicePixelRatio at 1.5, gate UnrealBloomPass and MeshPhysicalMaterial transmission behind an auto-detected or user-toggleable "quality" setting, use InstancedMesh for any repeated small elements (activation-flow particles, the neuron-population mode), and run the raster/membrane-trace plots on a plain 2D canvas overlay rather than in WebGL. This path is fully verified against the CDN allowlist, works from file://, stays comfortably inside the 16MB limit with zero embedded binary assets, and — done with the shaping/lobe/highlight details above — reads as an elegant, recognizable, purpose-built brain rather than a generic lumpy sphere, which is exactly the "simple but comprehensive" bar this project is aiming for.

neuron.model_choice:
Recommend the Izhikevich (2003) 2-variable model over LIF, AdEx, and Hodgkin-Huxley.

- Hodgkin-Huxley: ruled out. 4 state variables with multiple exp()-based gating functions per neuron, needs dt ~0.01-0.025ms for stability. For N=100-300 neurons in plain JS at 60fps this is too many transcendental-function evaluations per frame, and far more parameters than needed for the pedagogical goal.
- Plain LIF: too simple. Cannot natively produce bursting, chattering, or spike-frequency adaptation, so it can't show the "zoo" of cortical firing personalities (regular-spiking, fast-spiking, bursting, low-threshold-spiking) that makes exploring single-neuron dynamics interesting. Fine only as an optional "beginner" toggle before Izhikevich, not required.
- AdEx (adaptive exponential IF): reasonable middle ground with more biophysically-named parameters (adaptation time constant, threshold slope factor), but less standardized/famous for teaching, slightly more expensive (exponential term), and no real added clarity over Izhikevich at this scope.
- Izhikevich: 2 ODEs, ~5 flops/step, numerically cheap (trivially fits N=100-300 neurons at 60fps), and a single (a,b,c,d) parameter set reproduces essentially all known cortical/thalamic firing patterns (RS, FS, IB, CH, LTS, TC) -- exactly the "one simple recipe, many personalities" story that makes a good teaching demo. Izhikevich himself used this model for large-scale (tens of thousands of neurons) real-time cortex simulations, so it is proven for exactly this "efficient population of spiking neurons in software" use case. Main honesty caveat that must be stated in the UI: it is a phenomenological/fitted model, not conductance-based -- v and u do not correspond 1:1 to real ionic currents; they are abstractions tuned to reproduce the right spike patterns, not derived from channel biophysics.
neuron.equations_plain:
Core equations (verified against Izhikevich 2003 "Simple Model of Spiking Neurons," IEEE Trans. Neural Networks):

dv/dt = 0.04v^2 + 5v + 140 - u + I
du/dt = a(bv - u)
reset rule: if v >= 30 (mV) then v <- c and u <- u + d

Plain-English meaning of every term:
- v (membrane potential, mV): the neuron's voltage "state." Rises with input, and when it crosses +30 mV that counts as a spike (all-or-none event, not a graded signal).
- u (recovery variable): an abstract slow negative-feedback variable standing in for the combined effect of Na+ channel inactivation and slow K+ channel activation. It doesn't correspond to one real current; it's a fitted stand-in that produces the right shapes of behavior (adaptation, bursting, etc). Growing u pulls v back down and makes the neuron harder to fire again ("neuron getting tired").
- I (input current): everything driving the neuron -- injected/experimental current, incoming synaptic current from other simulated neurons, plus injected background noise standing in for the thousands of real synaptic inputs not simulated individually.
- The 0.04v^2 + 5v + 140 part: an empirically-fit quadratic (not derived from a channel model) chosen so the model's spike upstroke matches real cortical neuron behavior near threshold; it is why this model needs care in numerical integration (see pitfalls).
- a (recovery time scale, 1/ms): how fast u chases changes in v. Small a (e.g. 0.02) = slow recovery = can produce bursting or after-spike adaptation across a train; larger a (e.g. 0.1) = fast recovery = fast-spiking, minimal adaptation.
- b (sensitivity of u to sub-threshold v): controls how strongly small voltage wobbles below threshold recruit the recovery variable; larger b can produce low-threshold spiking / resonance-like behavior.
- c (reset voltage after a spike, mV): how far down v snaps immediately after a spike (models the fast K+-driven afterhyperpolarization). More negative c = deeper reset.
- d (after-spike jump added to u): the size of the "tiredness" bump added after each spike (models slower high-threshold Ca2+/K+ currents = spike-frequency adaptation). Larger d = each spike makes the next one harder = fewer spikes per burst, more adaptation.

Confirmed standard (a,b,c,d) presets from Izhikevich (2003), useful as named "neuron type" presets in the UI rather than raw sliders by default:
- Regular Spiking (RS, typical excitatory cortical pyramidal cell): a=0.02, b=0.2, c=-65, d=8
- Intrinsically Bursting (IB): a=0.02, b=0.2, c=-55, d=4
- Chattering (CH): a=0.02, b=0.2, c=-50, d=2
- Fast Spiking (FS, typical inhibitory interneuron): a=0.1, b=0.2, c=-65, d=2
- Low-Threshold Spiking (LTS): a=0.02, b=0.25, c=-65, d=2
- Thalamo-Cortical (TC): a=0.02, b=0.25, c=-65, d=0.05

default_params.description: dt = 0.5 ms per integration sub-step, using Izhikevich's own recommended stabilization trick: update v twice per 1 ms with half-steps (dt=0.5) while updating u once per full 1 ms, to tame the v^2 term (see pitfalls). Default run rate: 4 sub-steps (=2 ms of neural time) per animation frame at 60fps, giving ~120 ms neural-time per real second by default (~8x slower than biological real-time) -- exposed as a 'speed' slider from 0.25x to 8x so students can slow down to see individual spikes or speed up to see slow phenomena (adaptation, bursting cadence, oscillation build-up) unfold quickly. Population: N=150 total, 80/20 Dale's-law split = 120 excitatory (RS preset by default) + 30 inhibitory (FS preset by default) neurons. Connectivity: sparse random directed graph, each neuron's outgoing connections cover ~10% of the population chosen at random (~15 targets/neuron), fixed at network-build time (no rewiring), stored as adjacency lists in typed arrays. Synapses: simple exponential post-synaptic current kernel rather than instantaneous deltas, tau_E=5 ms (AMPA-like, excitatory), tau_I=10 ms (GABA-A-like, inhibitory); every neuron also gets an independent Gaussian background-noise current each step (mean 0, tunable std, default small) standing in for unmodeled synaptic bombardment (Destexhe-style 'high-conductance state' rationale). Synaptic delay: minimum 1 simulation step (>=0.5-1 ms) between presynaptic spike and postsynaptic current onset -- required to avoid pathological single-step whole-network lockstep synchrony from zero-delay coupling. Weight scaling: excitatory and inhibitory total synaptic drive are scaled to a rough balanced-network regime (Brunel-style) so the network sits in an asynchronous-irregular default state rather than silence or runaway synchrony; global 'excitatory drive' and 'GABA tone' sliders scale w_E and w_I respectively from that balanced baseline. All slider ranges must be clamped server-side/client-side to keep the network inside a non-diverging regime (see pitfalls) regardless of what combination a student picks.

neuromodulator_mappings.parameter_effect: Adds a small tonic depolarizing offset to the input current I (or raises b slightly) for a UI-labeled 'target' subpopulation only, optionally paired with a small multiplicative boost (1.0x-1.3x) to recurrent excitatory (E->E) synaptic weights in that same subpopulation. Keep the range small so it nudges excitability/gain rather than forcing runaway firing.
neuromodulator_mappings.plain_explanation: In real circuits, dopamine from VTA/SNc modulates excitability and synaptic gain in target neurons -- e.g. enhancing NMDA-mediated persistent activity in prefrontal cortex network models (Durstewitz & Seamans), with an inverted-U dose-response (too much is as bad as too little). In this sim, raising the Dopamine slider simply makes a highlighted 'target' group of neurons somewhat more excitable/responsive to input. It does NOT implement reward, prediction error, or any learning rule.
neuromodulator_mappings.confidence: Direction of the single-cell/circuit excitability effect is well-supported in computational modeling literature (Durstewitz & Seamans PFC models). The reduction to one global slider, the omission of receptor subtype (D1 vs D2) and dose-response nonlinearity (inverted-U), and especially the lack of any reward-learning loop are simplifications -- must be labeled explicitly so a student doesn't think this sim performs reinforcement learning.

neuromodulator_mappings.parameter_effect: Decrease the after-spike recovery increment d by up to ~50% from baseline (less spike-frequency adaptation), and separately scale down recurrent excitatory-to-excitatory (E->E) synaptic weights (e.g. to 50-70% of baseline) while leaving feedforward/external input drive untouched.
neuromodulator_mappings.plain_explanation: ACh from the basal forebrain suppresses M-current-like and other slow adaptation K+ currents, so neurons keep firing near their initial rate under sustained input instead of adapting down (documented mechanistically, e.g. attenuation of ERG-type K+ currents reducing spike-frequency adaptation and network correlation). ACh also presynaptically suppresses intracortical/recurrent excitatory synapses more than thalamic/afferent ones (Hasselmo's cholinergic modulation work), biasing a network from an 'internal replay' mode toward a 'feedforward sensory' mode. The slider lowers d and turns down recurrent E-E weights to reflect both effects.
neuromodulator_mappings.confidence: Well-supported mechanistically for both the adaptation-reduction effect and the recurrent-vs-afferent synapse suppression effect -- one of the more physiologically faithful sliders in this design, backed by named, citable primary literature (Hasselmo; ERG K+ current studies).

neuromodulator_mappings.parameter_effect: Apply a gain multiplier to each neuron's net synaptic + external current that is nonlinear in effect (amplifies already-suprathreshold/strong drive more than it amplifies subthreshold noise), and/or reduce the standard deviation of the background noise current -- both sharpen the network's effective input-output (f-I) curve.
neuromodulator_mappings.plain_explanation: Locus coeruleus noradrenaline release is classically modeled as increasing neural 'gain,' i.e. steepening the slope of the input-output curve, which raises the signal-to-noise ratio of target circuits (Servan-Schreiber, Printz & Cohen, Science 1990 -- 'A Network Model of Catecholamine Effects'; supported by later neural-gain/attention modeling, e.g. Eldar et al. eLife 2013). Raising the slider makes strong inputs produce proportionally stronger firing while weak/noisy inputs are relatively suppressed.
neuromodulator_mappings.confidence: Well-supported for the core gain/SNR mechanism -- this is a classic, frequently-cited, purpose-built computational result, arguably the single best-grounded neuromodulator mapping available. The further popular narrative linking this to 'arousal' or 'explore vs exploit' behavioral state is a reasonable but more interpretive extension; keep the slider's own description limited to gain/SNR and mark any arousal/exploration narrative as illustrative framing, not a modeled quantity.

neuromodulator_mappings.parameter_effect: Shift the excitation/inhibition set point by moving inhibitory-onto-excitatory and excitatory-onto-inhibitory weights modestly in opposite directions around baseline (a small bidirectional re-balancing), rather than a single unidirectional 'more/less excitable' dial.
neuromodulator_mappings.plain_explanation: Serotonin has been shown to fine-tune excitation/inhibition balance in cortical networks (e.g. Cerebral Cortex 2010, 'Serotoninergic Fine-Tuning of the Excitation-Inhibition Balance in Rat Visual Cortical Networks'), acting through multiple receptor subtypes whose net effect differs by context -- 5-HT1A is generally hyperpolarizing/inhibitory, 5-HT2A is often excitatory on some interneuron classes, so the real net direction is not one-size-fits-all. This sim represents serotonin as a knob that re-balances E vs I drive rather than a simple excitability dial. It explicitly does NOT model mood, wellbeing, depression, or SSRI-like pharmacology.
neuromodulator_mappings.confidence: Well-supported that 5-HT tunes E/I balance in cortical circuits (citable empirical/computational literature). The specific direction chosen for the slider, and especially the popular 'serotonin = mood/calm' association, are NOT modeled and must be labeled a metaphor / explicitly out of scope to avoid overclaiming -- this is one of the two weaker mappings in the set.

neuromodulator_mappings.parameter_effect: Directly multiply the inhibitory synaptic weight/conductance for all I->E and I->I connections by a single gain factor, optionally with a small added tonic hyperpolarizing/leak-like current on all neurons to represent extrasynaptic tonic GABA-A conductance.
neuromodulator_mappings.plain_explanation: This is the most literal slider in the set: it changes the actual strength of inhibitory synapses in the simulated network, which is mechanistically exactly what GABA-A receptor-mediated inhibition does in real cortex (about 20-30% of cortical neurons are GABAergic interneurons). Raising it shifts the network from asynchronous-irregular firing toward slower, more suppressed, or more oscillatory activity -- a direct, well-studied consequence of E/I balance shifts in spiking network models (Brunel-type balanced networks; PING/ING-style oscillations).
neuromodulator_mappings.confidence: Well-supported / direct mechanism, not a metaphor. This slider maps essentially 1:1 onto a real, well-characterized physiological parameter (inhibitory synaptic conductance) and its network-level consequences are standard, citable computational neuroscience (Brunel 2000 network states).

neuromodulator_mappings.parameter_effect: Composite, clearly-labeled illustrative slider: (a) increase background noise amplitude on all neurons, (b) modestly raise excitability (small added depolarizing current, or shift b) on a UI-labeled 'amygdala-like' subgroup, while (c) modestly suppress excitability (small hyperpolarizing offset) on a separately labeled 'hippocampus-like/regulatory' subgroup -- gesturing at documented opposite-direction, region-specific effects rather than one global excitability number.
neuromodulator_mappings.plain_explanation: Real cortisol/glucocorticoid effects on neurons are genuinely biphasic (fast non-genomic vs slow genomic signaling, on different timescales) and region-specific: basolateral amygdala neurons can become more excitable following corticosteroid exposure, while hippocampal circuits show more mixed, time-dependent effects (including changes via HCN1 channels and shifts in glutamatergic/GABAergic balance) rather than a simple excitability increase. This sim compresses all of that into one illustrative 'stress' slider nudging two labeled subgroups in opposite directions plus added noise, purely to convey the intuition that 'stress hormones don't just turn the brain up uniformly, they reweight different circuits differently and over different timescales.' It is not a quantitative or mechanistic stress model.
neuromodulator_mappings.confidence: LOW / pedagogical metaphor -- the weakest-grounded mapping in the set. Direction, magnitude, and time-course of real cortisol effects vary by brain region, receptor type, and time since stress onset in ways a single instantaneous slider cannot capture (confirmed across amygdala vs hippocampus literature, which shows opposite and time-dependent effects). Must carry the single most explicit 'illustrative only, not a real stress model' disclaimer of any slider in the UI.

neuron.population_design:
N = 150 point neurons total, split 80/20 by Dale's law: 120 excitatory (default preset: Regular Spiking) + 30 inhibitory (default preset: Fast Spiking) -- 80/20 is presented in the UI as "a common cortex-wide approximation," not a universal constant (real ratios vary by region/layer/species). Each neuron's identity (excitatory vs inhibitory) is fixed at network build time and it may ONLY make synapses of that one sign to every target it connects to (Dale's law) -- call this out explicitly in the UI since students often assume synapse sign can vary per-connection.

Connectivity: sparse random directed graph, not all-to-all. Each neuron connects to ~10% of the rest of the population chosen at random at build time (about 15 outgoing targets per neuron on average), stored as fixed adjacency lists in typed arrays (Int32Array indices + matching weight array) for fast iteration -- no runtime rewiring/plasticity in the base sim (keeps it explainable and avoids conflating this with a learning demo).

Synaptic transmission: not instantaneous voltage deltas -- use a simple exponentially-decaying post-synaptic current per neuron (one extra state variable per neuron, incremented on a presynaptic spike arrival and decaying each step), tau_E ~ 5 ms (AMPA-like) for excitatory sources and tau_I ~ 10 ms (GABA-A-like) for inhibitory sources. A minimum synaptic delay of one simulation step (>=0.5-1 ms) between presynaptic spike and postsynaptic current onset is required (see pitfalls) to avoid pathological zero-delay lockstep synchrony.

Background drive: every neuron receives an independent Gaussian noise current each step (mean 0, small tunable std), standing in for the thousands of real synaptic inputs per cortical neuron that aren't individually simulated (Destexhe-style "high-conductance/in-vivo-like" state rationale) -- flagged in the UI as a necessary simplification, not a literal biological noise source.

Numerical integration for 60fps in plain JS: dt = 0.5 ms; Izhikevich's own stabilization trick is used -- update v with two half-ms Euler sub-steps per full 1 ms tick while updating u once per full 1 ms tick -- to control the v^2 term's stiffness near spike threshold (see pitfalls; plain 1ms-step Euler on the raw equations is a known source of divergence). Default run rate: 4 sub-steps (2 ms neural time) per requestAnimationFrame call at 60fps (~120 ms neural-time/real-second by default), exposed via a "speed" slider (0.25x-8x) so a student can slow down to watch individual spikes or speed up to see slower phenomena (bursting cadence, adaptation, network oscillation build-up) within a reasonable wait. Performance: 150 neurons x ~15 synapses x a few flops/step x a handful of sub-steps/frame is trivial for JS at 60fps -- use Float32Array for all per-neuron state (v, u, synaptic current, noise seed) and pre-built Int32Array adjacency lists to avoid garbage-collection pauses from per-frame object allocation, and avoid re-allocating arrays inside the animation loop.

Weight/gain balancing: total excitatory and inhibitory synaptic drive are scaled from a rough balanced-network baseline (Brunel-style asynchronous-irregular regime) so the default network sits in a sustained, non-silent, non-runaway-synchronous firing state; the "excitatory drive" and "GABA tone" sliders scale w_E and w_I respectively away from that baseline, and both must be range-clamped so no slider combination can push the network into unbounded runaway firing or complete silence without at least a graceful, explained state (see pitfalls).
visualizations: Spike raster plot: y-axis = neuron index (excitatory neurons grouped/colored separately from inhibitory), x-axis = a scrolling time window (e.g. last 2-5 seconds of neural time); one tick/dot per spike. Must be drawn on an HTML canvas (not SVG/DOM nodes) for performance with hundreds of spikes accumulating over a scrolling window -- maintain a rolling spike buffer and redraw incrementally rather than re-rendering the whole history every frame.

Membrane potential (and recovery variable) trace: pick 1 (default) up to 3 user-selectable 'highlighted' neurons and plot v(t) over a rolling time window on a line chart, with the spike-and-reset visibly marked (sharp drop to c); optionally overlay u(t) as a second, differently-colored line so the 'recovery/tiredness' variable's role becomes visually tangible alongside voltage.

Population firing-rate plot (PSTH-style): a binned and smoothed spikes-per-second trace, plotted separately for the excitatory and inhibitory subpopulations over the same rolling time window, to make emergent phenomena (synchrony, oscillation, quiescence) visible at the population level rather than only spike-by-spike.

Phase portrait (v vs u) for the highlighted neuron, optional/advanced toggle: plot the live (v,u) trajectory in the v-u plane, optionally overlaid with the two nullclines (dv/dt=0: u = 0.04v^2+5v+140+I; du/dt=0: u = b*v) so a curious student can see geometrically why/when a spike is imminent. Cheap to compute (closed-form nullclines), high pedagogical payoff, but needs its own short explanation panel since phase portraits are unfamiliar to most students -- keep behind an 'advanced' toggle rather than shown by default.

Optional/secondary: a small population 'heat' view -- neurons laid out on a compact grid or ring, node color/brightness driven by each neuron's recent (e.g. last 100ms) firing rate, updated every frame. Nice at-a-glance 'network is active here' feel; strictly secondary to the raster and rate plots, and must not be captioned in a way that implies it shows 'thoughts' or cognition (see pitfalls).
explanations_to_include: What a spike is: an all-or-none threshold-crossing event, not a graded/analog signal -- contrast explicitly with the continuous membrane-potential trace shown right next to the raster.
What the membrane potential v represents physically (voltage across the neuron's membrane) and what resting potential / depolarization / threshold mean in plain terms.

What the recovery variable u represents: an abstract 'tiredness'/negative-feedback stand-in for combined Na+ inactivation and slow K+ activation -- explicitly NOT a single real physical current, to prevent the misconception that u = potassium current.

Plain-English meaning of each of a, b, c, d individually (see equations_plain), presented primarily via named neuron-type presets (RS/FS/IB/CH/LTS/TC) with an 'advanced' toggle exposing the raw sliders for students who want to explore the parameter space directly.

What the input current I represents: an 'electrode/injected current' analogy for the tonic/external part, plus an explicit note that the added background noise is a simplification standing in for thousands of unmodeled real synaptic inputs, not a claim that real neurons have literal random noise generators.

Dale's law, stated explicitly as a real biological constraint (not just an implementation detail): a real neuron is either excitatory or inhibitory to ALL of its postsynaptic targets, it cannot switch sign connection-by-connection -- flagged because this is a common student misconception.

What excitatory vs inhibitory population balance (E/I ratio) means and why cortex is commonly approximated as ~80% excitatory / ~20% inhibitory, with a caveat that real ratios vary by region/layer/species.
How to read the raster plot: one dot = one spike from one neuron at one moment; rows = distinct neurons; columns = time -- explicitly avoid narrating it as 'the brain thinking.'

What population firing rate means (spikes/second averaged over a short window and over neurons) and, at a plain-language level, why recurrent excitation/inhibition timing can produce visible oscillations or synchrony in the rate trace.

Why the simulation advances in small discrete time steps (dt) rather than continuously, and briefly why too large a step causes visible instability -- kept short/intuitive, not a numerical-methods lecture.

For EVERY neuromodulator slider, a fixed two-part inline explanation pattern: 'In real neurons/circuits: <one-sentence mechanism with citation-worthy claim>' followed by 'In this simulation we simplify it as: <exact parameter(s) being changed>', plus a visible honesty badge per slider (e.g. Well-supported mechanism / Simplified but directionally supported / Illustrative metaphor only) -- this pairing should be a structural UI requirement, not just optional prose, given the project's 'every knob explained + flag metaphors' goal.

A persistent, hard-to-miss disclaimer (e.g. a small fixed banner or an always-visible 'About this model' panel) stating: this is a simplified pedagogical model of ~150 point neurons, not a real brain simulation; real human cortex has on the order of tens of billions of neurons with vastly more cell-type and connectivity diversity; real synapses have complex plasticity not modeled here; real neuromodulators act via multiple distinct receptor subtypes with region- and time-specific effects that a single global slider cannot represent.

Explicit statement that the Izhikevich model is phenomenological/fitted, not conductance-based like Hodgkin-Huxley -- v and u reproduce the right spiking behavior without corresponding 1:1 to identified ion channels.

A short note distinguishing 'simulation speed' (the UI speed multiplier / how much neural time passes per rendered frame) from 'biological realism' -- speeding up the sim to see slow phenomena faster is a UI convenience, not a claim about how fast real neurons operate.
pitfalls: Numerical instability from the v^2 term: naive single Euler step at dt=1ms on the raw Izhikevich equations can make v diverge/blow up near and after threshold crossing. Mitigation (from Izhikevich's own recommendation): split each 1ms tick into two 0.5ms sub-steps for updating v while updating u once per full 1ms tick; additionally hard-clamp v into a safe range (e.g. no lower than about -100 to -120 mV, and check for spike/reset before v is allowed to run away past +30) on every sub-step, not just at the end of a full tick.

Extreme slider combinations (student cranks input current, or 'advanced' a/b/c/d far outside Izhikevich's tested regimes) can push the model into non-biological behavior: infinite firing, numerical overflow, or NaN state. All sliders must be range-clamped to keep the system inside a non-diverging regime, and the update loop must defensively check isFinite(v)/isFinite(u) each step and reset a neuron to a safe resting state if it goes non-finite, rather than letting NaN silently propagate through the raster/rate plots.

Spike detection at large dt can overshoot v well past +30mV before the threshold check runs, biasing spike timing/counting in the raster if only checked once per full tick -- check the threshold condition after each integration sub-step, not only once per rendered frame or once per full 1ms tick.

Zero synaptic delay in a recurrent network is a common source of a purely numerical (not physiological) artifact: with strong enough weights, fully instantaneous coupling can make many neurons fire in perfect lockstep within a single simulation step. A minimum 1-step (>=0.5-1ms) synaptic delay is required both for numerical realism and to avoid this pathological synchrony artifact.

Weight/scale mismatch as network size or E/I sliders change: total synaptic drive onto a neuron scales with in-degree x weight, so if excitatory and inhibitory total drive aren't kept roughly balanced (Brunel-style), the network can flip between total silence and runaway synchronous firing as a student adjusts N, connectivity, or the excitatory/GABA-tone sliders -- design the weight-scaling formula so it stays near a balanced regime across the intended slider ranges, and clamp the extremes.

Do not narrate simulated activity in mentalistic terms: avoid phrases like 'the network is thinking,' 'this IS the fear circuit,' or 'the neuron feels reward.' The population is a generic, unwired-to-any-real-circuit toy network with a few labeled subgroups for neuromodulator sliders -- it does not replicate actual amygdala/VTA/hippocampal connectivity, so all copy should say 'illustrates a mechanism associated with X' rather than claiming the sim IS structure X.

Do not frame the Dopamine slider as implementing reward-prediction-error, temporal-difference learning, or any form of learning/plasticity unless a real reward+learning loop is actually built -- if the base sim has no synaptic plasticity, the dopamine slider must be described purely as an excitability/gain modulator on a labeled subgroup, otherwise it overclaims a mechanism (RPE/TD learning) that is well-documented in the literature but not actually present in this simulation.

Serotonin and cortisol/stress are the two weakest-grounded mappings (confirmed via literature check: 5-HT's net E/I effect is receptor- and context-dependent rather than unidirectional; cortisol effects are genuinely biphasic, region-specific, and time-dependent, with amygdala and hippocampus documented to respond differently). These two sliders must visibly carry a stronger 'illustrative metaphor' disclaimer than GABA tone, acetylcholine, or noradrenaline, which are more directly grounded -- treating all six sliders with the same confidence badge would misrepresent how well-supported each one actually is.

The Izhikevich model itself is phenomenological (curve-fit), not conductance-based -- avoid any copy implying u 'is' a specific ionic current (e.g. 'this is the potassium current') since it is a fitted abstraction that reproduces the right dynamics rather than a biophysically derived quantity.

Do not conflate the UI's simulation-speed multiplier with a claim about biological realism or timing accuracy -- speeding up/slowing down neural-time-per-frame is purely a viewing convenience and should be labeled as such, not presented as if it reflects how fast real neurons actually operate.

draft.architecture:
Single index.html, ~2.5-3.5k lines, zero build step, opens via file:// or any static host. One <script type="importmap"> (must precede the module script) maps three, three/addons/, and simplex-noise to pinned jsdelivr npm-proxy URLs (three@0.170.0, simplex-noise@4.0.3) — cdnjs is never used for addons since it only mirrors three's core build (verified by the tech scout). Exactly one <script type="module"> holds all app logic; this is not a style choice but a hard constraint — file:// blocks relative-path imports of a second local .js file (CORS), while CDN imports work because they're genuine https:// fetches. Internally the module is organized as clearly commented sections (data → math/geometry helpers → scene/renderer → interaction/raycasting → three mode controllers → shared UI chrome → render loop → boot), not as literal ES module files. Rendering is a single WebGL canvas full-bleed behind an HTML/CSS overlay UI layer (fixed/absolute-positioned glass panels); the neuron-simulation plots are plain 2D <canvas> elements composited over the WebGL canvas, not WebGL geometry. No backend, no build tooling, no external fonts required (system font stack) though Google Fonts may be added via the allowed fonts.googleapis.com/gstatic.com pair if a more distinctive typeface is wanted.

DECISION — procedural brain, not an embedded asset: The tech scout checked every realistic free source (Neuro.Wiki, NIH 3DPX-001944, Z-Anatomy/BodyParts3D, Sketchfab uploads) and each one fails at least one hard requirement simultaneously — a genuinely permissive license (several are CC BY-SA / CC BY-NC-SA, legally awkward to bundle into a shareable single-file artifact), true pre-segmentation into separate per-structure meshes rather than one fused blob, a no-manual-pipeline direct download, and a base64-safe size under the 16MB artifact cap. Compounding this, the sandbox's CSP blocks any live fetch of an external .glb/.gltf/texture/font outright — even a perfect asset could only be used by hand base64-embedding it at authoring time and loading via GLTFLoader.parse(arrayBuffer), which bloats the file and kills iterability for zero net benefit over building it procedurally. Building hemispheres as noise-displaced IcosahedronGeometry ellipsoids, a rippled cerebellum, a lathe/cylinder brainstem, and ~14 simple-primitive subcortical structures (spheres, TubeGeometry curves for hippocampus/caudate/corpus callosum) stays fully inside the CDN allowlist, needs zero embedded binaries, is trivially editable, and — with the shaping/parcellation/highlight details specified below — reads as an elegant, recognizable, purpose-built brain rather than a generic lumpy sphere, which matches the "simple but comprehensive" bar better than any asset path that was actually available.
draft.data_model:
All content is embedded as plain JS object/array literals transcribed directly from the research JSON (no runtime fetch — everything is static data baked into the file):

REGIONS: keyed by id (v1, v4, mt_v5, ffa, a1, wernicke, broca, s1, m1, ppc, dlpfc, vmpfc_ofc, acc, insula, corpus_callosum, thalamus, hypothalamus, amygdala, hippocampus, striatum, globus_pallidus, stn, nucleus_accumbens, vta, substantia_nigra, cerebellum, locus_coeruleus, raphe_nuclei — 28 total). Each entry keeps the research's fields verbatim (name, group, one_liner, functions[], lesion_effects, approx_location, key_connections[], famous_case_or_evidence?) plus three build-time-only fields added during Step 6/10: `kind` ('cortical-region' | 'subcortical' | 'brainstem' | 'cerebellum' | 'commissure'), `position` (Vector3 in model space, either the centroid read off the built mesh for subcortical/discrete objects, or a representative point for cortical regionId zones), and `meshRefs` (populated at build time — one or two Object3D refs for paired structures).

CORTICAL PARCELLATION MAP: a small pure function `regionIdForVertex(theta, phi, side)` returning one of the 12 cortical region ids (v1, v4, mt_v5, ffa, a1, wernicke/broca on the language-dominant side only — see note below, s1, m1, ppc, dlpfc, vmpfc_ofc, acc) from hand-tuned angular boundaries against the pre-displacement unit-sphere position. Wernicke's/Broca's are shown only on the left hemisphere (with a one-line note on the right hemisphere's homologous patch: "usually less specialized for language"), reflecting the ~95-99% left-lateralization the content notes as typical-not-universal. Insula and corpus_callosum are NOT part of this attribute (see below).

PATHWAYS: array of 8 scenario objects (recognize_face, recall_word, fear_response, making_decision, reading_sentence, motor_skill_learning, attention_shift, sleep_consolidation), each with id, title, scenario_sentence, steps[] (region_ids[], approx_ms, what_happens, why_it_matters, evidence_or_method), and accuracy_caveats (rendered as a permanently visible "how literally to take this" note under the step content, not hidden in a tooltip).

GLOSSARY: array of 38 {term, plain_definition} entries, used two ways: (a) linkTerms(html) auto-wraps any occurrence of a term (longest-match-first, word-boundary regex, case-insensitive) in the dynamically-rendered explain/atlas/neuron text into a clickable `<span class="term" data-term="...">`; (b) a full A-Z browsable list inside the "How this works" drawer as a coverage safety net independent of incidental text matches.

NEURON_PRESETS: the 6 named (a,b,c,d) sets (RS, IB, CH, FS, LTS, TC) plus their one-line behavioral description, used as the default UI (dropdown) with an "advanced" toggle exposing raw a/b/c/d sliders clamped to safe ranges.

NEUROMOD_DEFS: array of 6 {name, parameter_effect (exact simulation mapping), plain_explanation, confidence} entries transcribed from the research, each rendered with the fixed two-part pattern ("In real neurons/circuits: ..." / "In this simulation we simplify it as: ...") plus a visible honesty badge derived from `confidence` (Well-supported / Simplified-but-directional / Illustrative metaphor only — Serotonin and Cortisol get the weakest badge per the research's explicit confidence notes).

ACCURACY_PITFALLS: the 13-item list from research, rendered verbatim (lightly copy-edited) as a "Common misconceptions" section in the "How this works" drawer.

Runtime-only state (not persisted, no localStorage needed since nothing here demands cross-session memory): activeMode, atlas.selectedRegionId, atlas.lesionedIds (Set), atlas.lesionModeOn, pathway.activeId/activeStepIndex/isPlaying/speedMultiplier, neuron.Float32Array state arrays (v,u,Isyn per neuron), neuron.adjacency (Int32Array), neuron.sliderValues (6 neuromodulators + speed + N/connectivity if exposed), neuron.highlightedNeuronIndices, quality.level (auto-detected + user override), glossary.openTerm.
draft.ui_layout: Full-viewport 3-zone layout: (1) a fixed topbar (~56px) — app name/logo mark on the left, a 3-pill mode switcher centered (Pathways / Atlas / Neurons, each pill tinted with its accent color when active), and a right cluster with a quality toggle (Auto/High/Low), a "?" button opening the How-this-works drawer, and a small keyboard-shortcut hint; (2) the WebGL canvas fills the remaining viewport as the base layer, with OrbitControls (rotate/pan/zoom, damped) always live except a widescreen-only micro-hint on first load ("drag to rotate, scroll to zoom, click a region"); (3) floating glass panels overlaid on the canvas rather than a hard sidebar split, so the brain stays large and central: a left panel (~340px, collapsible via a chevron) holds the mode-specific control list (pathway scenario picker + transport controls, or atlas region search/list + lesion toggle, or neuron presets + neuromodulator sliders), and a bottom-right "Explain this" card (~380px wide, max ~50vh, scrollable) is always present and re-populates live with whatever is hovered/selected/animating — this is the one panel that never disappears across modes, giving the app a consistent anchor. In Pathway mode a slim horizontal timeline scrubber docks along the bottom edge showing step markers and the current approx_ms readout. In Neuron mode the left panel's lower half is replaced by the three stacked 2D-canvas plots (raster, membrane+recovery trace, population rate), with the advanced phase-portrait plot behind a collapsed "Advanced" disclosure. The glossary popover is a small fixed-width card that appears anchored near the clicked term (flips side near viewport edges) with the definition and a subtle "part of glossary" chevron linking into the full drawer list. The How-this-works drawer slides in from the right at ~420px wide, full height, with its own internal tab/anchor nav (Rendering / Timing model / Neuron equations / Metaphor vs. physiology / Full glossary). Keyboard: number keys 1/2/3 switch modes, arrow keys step through the active pathway or move focus through the atlas region list, space toggles pathway play/pause, Escape closes any open popover/drawer.
draft.visual_design: Dark, glassy, minimal — one calm neutral base so switching modes doesn't jar, with exactly one accent color per mode carrying all the "this mode is active" signaling: Pathways = a cool cyan/teal (--accent-pathway), Atlas = a violet/orchid (--accent-atlas), Neurons = a warm amber (--accent-neuron). Base palette: near-black ink background (#0a0b0f range) for the page behind the canvas, panels as translucent dark glass (rgba background ~0.55-0.65 alpha over a subtle backdrop-filter: blur(16px), 1px hairline border at ~8-12% white, soft outer shadow) so the 3D brain reads through faintly at panel edges. Brain materials: cortex hemispheres in a cool, slightly translucent blue-gray (MeshPhysicalMaterial, opacity ~0.3, low roughness) so gyral folding is legible while subcortical structures glow through from beneath; each subcortical structure gets its own small distinct emissive-tinted color (thalamus pale gold, amygdala warm red, hippocampus amber, striatum violet, etc.) chosen for maximum distinguishability at a glance, not for anatomical realism — documented as such. Selection/hover state = a soft rim-light glow in the active mode's accent color (via emissive intensity lerp), never a hard outline, keeping the "elegant" register. Typography: one geometric/humanist sans for all UI chrome (system-ui stack, or Inter/Space Grotesk via Google Fonts if a more distinctive brand feel is wanted) at a restrained size scale (13-15px body, 11-12px labels/badges, larger 20-24px for pathway scenario titles and region names), plus a monospace face for every numeric readout (ms timers, mV values, slider numbers, spike counts) so "live data" is visually distinct from prose. Generous whitespace: panel internal padding ~20-24px, list-item spacing ~12px, never more than ~65-70 characters per line of explanatory prose. Honesty badges (Well-supported / Simplified-directional / Illustrative metaphor) get their own small muted chip style (not accent-colored) so they read as neutral metadata, not part of the color-coded mode system. No skeuomorphism, no gradients beyond very subtle panel-edge glass sheen, no more than the three defined accents plus the neutral grayscale ramp anywhere in the UI.

modes.name: Cognitive Pathway Journeys
modes.behavior: User picks one of 8 preset scenarios from the left panel (Recognizing a Face, Recalling a Word/Name, Fear Response, Making a Decision, Reading a Sentence, Learning a Motor Skill, Shifting Attention, Sleep & Memory Consolidation). Transport controls (play/pause/prev/next) and a bottom timeline scrubber step through that scenario's ordered steps; each step highlights its region(s) with an accent-colored emissive glow, camera eases toward the relevant area, and (for steps after the first) a small InstancedMesh pulse travels along a CatmullRomCurve3 between the previous and current step's region centroid to visualize 'activation flowing'. approx_ms is shown as a running readout on the scrubber.
modes.explanation_surface: The persistent Explain panel shows the current step's what_happens, why_it_matters, and evidence_or_method, with every technical term auto-linked to the glossary; the pathway's scenario_sentence sits at the top and its accuracy_caveats sits in a permanently visible muted note beneath the step content (not hidden), since several pathways explicitly flag their ms values as schematic order-of-engagement rather than literal timings.

modes.name: Atlas Explore
modes.behavior: A searchable/filterable list of all 28 regions (grouped by the research's `group` field — occipital lobe, temporal lobe, basal ganglia, brainstem, etc.) sits in the left panel; clicking a list item or clicking the region directly in the 3D view selects it, eases the camera toward it, and applies the accent-colored highlight. A 'Lesion mode' toggle switches click behavior from 'select' to 'lesion': clicking a region instead dims it to a flat gray, drops its opacity, and marks it with a small 'LESIONED' badge, while its lesion_effects text becomes the headline of the Explain panel; multiple regions can be lesioned at once (a 'reset all' button clears them) to let a student explore combinations informally.
modes.explanation_surface: The Explain panel renders the selected region's full card: name, one_liner, functions (bulleted), lesion_effects, approx_location, key_connections (each connection name is itself clickable and jumps/selects that region), and famous_case_or_evidence when present — all text passed through the glossary auto-linker.

modes.name: Parametric Neuron Simulation
modes.behavior: A population of 150 Izhikevich point neurons (120 excitatory/RS default + 30 inhibitory/FS default, Dale's-law-fixed at build time, ~10% random sparse connectivity, exponential synaptic kernels, 1-step minimum synaptic delay, per-neuron Gaussian background noise) runs continuously via a fixed dt=0.5ms sub-step accumulator (u updated once per full 1ms), at a default of 4 sub-steps per animation frame with a 0.25x-8x speed slider. A neuron-type preset dropdown (RS/IB/CH/FS/LTS/TC) picks the (a,b,c,d) of up to 3 user-highlighted neurons, with an 'advanced' toggle exposing raw a/b/c/d sliders (range-clamped to a non-diverging regime). Six neuromodulator sliders (Dopamine, Acetylcholine, Noradrenaline, Serotonin, GABA tone, Cortisol/stress) each apply the exact parameter mapping specified in the research to labeled subgroups or global weights.
modes.explanation_surface: The left panel's lower half hosts three live 2D-canvas plots (spike raster colored by E/I, membrane-potential + recovery-variable trace for the highlighted neuron(s), population firing-rate PSTH for E vs I) plus a collapsed 'advanced' v-u phase portrait with nullclines; every neuromodulator slider shows its fixed two-part explanation ('In real neurons/circuits: ...' / 'In this simulation we simplify it as: ...') plus a visible confidence badge, and a persistent disclaimer banner states this is ~150 point neurons on a fitted (non-conductance-based) model, not a real brain, with Dale's law, spikes-as-threshold-events, and the dt/speed-vs-realism distinctions called out per the research's explanations_to_include list.
